instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Atmospheric perspective — Image Wiki
answer:
Ansel Adams, Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, between 1933 and 1942. National Archives. Public domain, US government work.
That arithmetic in one frame, in black and white, so no colour distracts you. Rank four things by how dark their darkest part is: the butte filling the foreground has true blacks and countable rubble; the walls across the middle are mid-grey with the rock banding still readable; the far rim is a flat light band; the mountains on the skyline are barely a shade darker than the sky.
Note the order things were lost in. Shadow detail went first — the far rim has shape but no shadows in it — and the fine detail followed because the contrast carrying it went. Nothing here is blue, and the cue is at full strength.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Atmospheric perspective — Image Wiki
answer:
Clean dry air: a blue veil spent over tens of kilometres
Fog: a white veil spent over about a hundred metres


Left: Gaurav Kapatia, hills at Chopta, Uttarakhand, CC BY-SA 4.0. Right: Dietmar Rabich, trees in fog near Dülmen, CC BY-SA 4.0. Two air masses, one cue.
Left, clean mountain air. The ridge on the right is dark green with individual conifers you can pick out; behind it four or five more ridges climb toward the horizon, each paler, bluer and flatter than the last, until one is barely separable from the sky. The sky does it too — deepest at the top of the frame, palest at the horizon, because a horizontal line of sight goes through far more air than an upward one.
Right, a farm track in fog, with trees of the same kind and size along it. The nearest is brown-black with countable twigs, the next is already a grey outline, and within four or five the row has dissolved into white. Same ladder, spent over about a hundred metres instead of tens of kilometres, because this air is carrying vastly more water — and the veil is white, not blue. Check the sky in the picture first, then check whether the far things are heading toward it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Atmospheric perspective — Image Wiki
answer:
Albert Bierstadt, Among the Sierra Nevada, California, 1868, public domain.
The same ladder built by hand, in colour. The trees on the right bank are green and near-black in their shadows, with branches you could count; the slopes in the middle distance have lost most of their green; the peaks at the back are a narrow band of light values with no nameable detail. Compare the darkest spot in those peaks with the darkest spot in the foreground trees — the mountains never come close. Distance is not pushing them toward black, it is pushing them toward the sky, and once two things reach the same value the boundary between them disappears.
The veil here is warm, not blue: the light breaking through the cloud is golden, and haze takes the colour of the light it scatters.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Balance — Image Wiki
answer:
Symmetrical: Perugino, Christ Giving the Keys of the Kingdom to St. Peter, 1481–83
Asymmetrical: Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, 1871


Perugino, Christ Giving the Keys of the Kingdom to St. Peter, Sistine Chapel, 1481–83. James McNeill Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, 1871 (Musée d'Orsay). Both public domain.
Perugino mirrors the whole field about a vertical line: domed temple on the axis, a triumphal arch at the same height and the same distance out on each side, small knots of figures echoing each other left and right in the middle distance, even a pair of slim trees. Fold the architecture down the middle and the halves land on top of each other.
That mirror has a consequence worth knowing. Whatever sits on the axis is now the only thing in the picture with no twin, so it becomes enormously important by default — here the temple doorway, and below it the key changing hands between Christ and the kneeling Peter.
Whistler balances things that do not match. The heavy mass is the black dress on the right; nothing on the left resembles it, and it is answered instead by the dark patterned curtain running down the left edge, plus the small framed print high up. Between the two dark edges sits a large plain grey wall carrying almost no weight at all. Cover the curtain with your thumb and the whole picture slides right.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Balance — Image Wiki
answer:
Garbhadhātu (Taizōkai) Mandala, Womb World, Japan, Heian period, late 9th century, colours on silk. Public domain.
Radial balance in its purest form. There are several hundred figures here and the weight is spread almost perfectly evenly — yet your eye does not wander, it drops straight to the small seated Buddha at the middle of the eight-petalled lotus.
It is barely larger than the figures around it and carries no stronger colour. It wins mostly because every ring in the picture is concentric with it, so the whole structure points inward. This is the one balance scheme that hands you a focal point for free, which is also why it is used for sacred images and clock faces and almost nothing else — you cannot put the emphasis anywhere but the middle.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Balance — Image Wiki
answer:
Edgar Degas, In a Café (L'Absinthe), 1875–76 (Musée d'Orsay). Public domain.
Deliberate imbalance, done by a painter who could balance a frame in his sleep. Both people are shoved into the upper right; the entire lower left is empty marble table top, a pale wedge with a newspaper spar cutting across the corner. Squint and the mass is one lump in one quadrant.
Two things stop it recovering. The pair sit at separate tables, so nothing joins them across the frame; and neither looks at anything inside the picture — her gaze drops out of the bottom edge, his goes off to the right, past the border. There is nothing on the empty side to answer the weight and no line of sight to tie the halves together.
The result is the tipping feeling described at the top of this article, and it is the subject: two people sitting side by side with nothing between them.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Beyond Latin — Image Wiki
answer:
W3C, Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements, §Cursive text → Joining Forms. Reproduced under the W3C Document License: "W3C liability, trademark and permissive document license rules apply."
One letter — meem — four glyphs. Not four styles to choose between: software has to pick the right one from context. The initial form joins leftwards only, the medial joins on both sides, the final joins rightwards only. ALREQ also defines right-joining letters with only two forms, and non-joining letters with one.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Beyond Latin — Image Wiki
answer:
W3C, Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements, §Text alignment & justification → Kashida. Reproduced under the W3C Document License.
Read right to left. Each row is one word, an arrow, then the same word with a kashida applied: a horizontal connection inside it has been drawn out. No space changed width — the word itself got longer.
ALREQ is careful about limits: too much kashida, or several close together, gives uneven colour, and some typefaces need curved kashidas, which is much harder to implement.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Beyond Latin — Image Wiki
answer:
W3C, Requirements for Japanese Text Layout, Figure 18, §2.3 Vertical Writing Mode and Horizontal Writing Mode. Reproduced under the W3C Document License.
The same sentence twice. Top: vertical mode — characters run down, columns advance right to left. Bottom: horizontal, left to right. Follow the grey arrows.
Now look at the blue cells. Every character fills an identical square, which is why one set of type serves both directions. It is also why "45 to 75 characters per line" cannot be imported: JLREQ specifies a page as a kihon-hanmen, a grid fixed by character size, direction, line length, lines per page and line gap. Characters-per-line advice assumes proportional letters of varying width. There are none here.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Beyond Latin — Image Wiki
answer:
Ruby: the reading, set alongside
Warichu: a note split into two small lines inside the line


W3C, Requirements for Japanese Text Layout, Figures 105 and 145. Reproduced under the W3C Document License.
Left — ruby: small characters attached to base characters to give their reading; when it spells out how to pronounce a kanji it is furigana. JLREQ puts it to the right of the base characters in vertical mode and above them in horizontal mode, and defines three layouts with separate rules — mono-ruby per character, group-ruby across a run, jukugo-ruby for compounds. JLREQ describes ruby as frequently used in modern documents including newspapers: ordinary text, not a specialism.
Right — warichu, an inline cutting note: two lines of smaller characters set inside the body line, splitting it in half. Less frequent, but standard in reference books and travel guides. No Latin device does this.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: When a chart lies — Image Wiki
answer:
Office for National Statistics service manual, chart elements. Open Government Licence v3.0. The red text is the ONS's annotation of its own legend specification.
Follow the rising blue line and the falling green one. They cross cleanly in late 2020 — and their shaded 95% confidence intervals overlap right through that crossing, pulling apart only near the end. Strip the bands out and the same three lines assert a handover on a date the data cannot pin down.
The bands widen to the right, which is the honest shape for anything projected forward. The Urban Institute's version is blunter: a poll giving a candidate 54% with a margin of ±4 points has not put them ahead of a rival on 50%.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: When a chart lies — Image Wiki
answer:
Office for National Statistics service manual, chart elements. Open Government Licence v3.0.
Four honest habits in one picture. The two series that matter are labelled at the end of their own lines, so nothing has to be matched against a legend; the other four are left grey, which is Visual hierarchy doing the work a legend would have done badly. A dashed reference line marks a date and a shaded range marks a period, each with a short annotation saying what it was — the ONS caps these at ten to twelve words. The source sits under the chart. The y-axis runs from zero to past the highest point, so the full relevant range is there.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Choosing a chart — Image Wiki
answer:
Office for National Statistics service manual, chart elements. Open Government Licence v3.0. The red text is the ONS's own annotation of its gridline specification.
A ranking chart doing the small things right. It is a bar rather than a column because the category names are long sentences. The bars run from highest to lowest so neighbouring values can be compared without hunting — the ONS is explicit that alphabetical order is the wrong default — except for "Other service activities", which is plotted last regardless of size because it is not a real category. The axis starts at zero, values are labelled on the bars, and the source is stated under the chart.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to choose colours — Image Wiki
answer:
Claude Monet, Impression, soleil levant, 1872. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. Public domain.
The extreme case of the lever. The sun disc covers about a thousandth of the canvas, plus a thin column of the same orange broken across the water. Everything else — masts, cranes, the whole sky below the top band — is low-chroma blue-green grey.
Measure it instead of guessing. The disc runs about L* 68 at chroma 67, the mist either side of it L* 50 at chroma 10. Follow the orange column down onto the water and the lightness advantage nearly disappears — those strokes sit at L* 52 against water at L* 45 — while the chroma gap holds at roughly 48 against 15. Chroma, not value, is what points this picture at one spot.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to choose colours — Image Wiki
answer:
Two hues, low chroma: Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Silver — Chelsea, 1871
Three hues, high chroma: Van Gogh, The Night Café, 1888


Two public-domain paintings seventeen years apart, differing mainly in how much chroma is allowed and over how much area. Right: Yale University Art Gallery.
Whistler works one hue. River, far bank, sky and the moored barge are all a blue, and the picture is separated by lightness alone. Count the exceptions: two orange lamp notes, each a few millimetres of paint with a short reflection under it. Those are the only marks in the frame with any chroma, and they carry the whole evening.
Van Gogh does the opposite deliberately, and wrote to Theo that he had tried to express "the terrible passions of humanity" with red and green. The wall is a large field of near-maximum red, the ceiling and billiard table near-maximum green, the floor yellow. No area yields, so the eye is pulled round the room and never settles. Not a mistake — it is what large opposed chroma does.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to choose colours — Image Wiki
answer:
Paul Gauguin, Bouquet de fleurs, 1897. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. Public domain. Handprint uses this painting to work through colour design, so it is the fairest test of the schemes.
Name the palette and you get scarlet, umber, ochre, blue-grey — which sounds like a scheme and tells you nothing. The information is in the area and the chroma. Measured off this reproduction, the scarlet marks cover about 3.5 per cent of the canvas and 94 per cent of the surface sits below chroma 45: the ochre wall is chroma 26, the blue-grey cloth 12, the dark leaves under 10.
Handprint then ran the experiment. He rotated every hue in this painting one step around the circle, once toward magenta and once toward green. The "scheme" is identical in all three versions and both rotations fall apart: one trades the scarlet-against-umber punch for a limp red-against-maroon, the other turns the light sickly. If the relationship were doing the work, spinning the dial would be free.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The colour of the light — Image Wiki
answer:
Direct sun: Rouen Cathedral, West Façade, Sunlight
Diffuse sky: Rouen Cathedral, West Façade


Claude Monet, two canvases from the Rouen Cathedral series, both 1894, both public domain. Left: National Gallery of Art, Washington. Same building, same viewpoint, same grey limestone — Monet painted the series to record the light changing.
Left, in direct sun, the stone comes out cream and pale gold, while the recesses of the three portals — cut off from the sun, lit only by sky — go blue-violet.
Right, with the sun off the façade, that same stone reads lavender-blue almost everywhere and the sky becomes the warm note, a pale cream. What direct light remains is the salmon-pink down the ribs of the left tower. Warm and cool have swapped sides without anything in the scene moving.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The colour of the light — Image Wiki
answer:
Claude Monet, The Magpie, 1868–69. Musée d'Orsay, Paris. Public domain.
Snow is the cleanest test surface there is, because its local colour is near-white: any colour you can see in it came from the light. Follow the shadow the gate casts down and to the right across the foreground, and the shadowed face of the snow-drifted wall at the far left. Both are unmistakably blue-lilac while the snow beside them is a warm cream — there is no neutral grey in the snow anywhere.
Not the same light dimmed. The lit snow sees the low sun plus the sky; the shadowed snow sees only the sky, and reports its colour faithfully.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The colour of the light — Image Wiki
answer:
Georges de La Tour, The Penitent Magdalene with a Night Light, c. 1640–45. Musée du Louvre. Public domain (Web Gallery of Art reproduction).
The single-source case, with no cool fill at all. Read the light off the neutral: her chemise is white linen. Where it faces the lamp, high on her chest, it is cream; along her far sleeve, amber-gold; beyond that, brown and then black. Not one blue note in the whole garment. With no second light the dark side of every form falls away to nothing, which is why a room lit by one flame reads as a far smaller world than a sunlit street.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Hue, value and chroma — Image Wiki
answer:
Frederic Leighton, Flaming June, 1895. Museo de Arte de Ponce. Public domain.
One hue held across most of a canvas while the other two dials move. Follow any fold from its lit crest into the crease beside it. Sampled off the dress, the palest crests average L* 65 at chroma 38 and the deepest creases L* 16 at chroma 23 — and the strongest orange in the garment is neither. It sits in the middle, at L* 46 with chroma 67.
Chroma peaks in the mid-values and falls toward both ends, exactly as the right-hand panel above predicts. The dull orange in the deep folds is not weak colour; it is the correct colour for that value.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Hue, value and chroma — Image Wiki
answer:
Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889. Museum of Modern Art, New York. Public domain.
Two hues at nearly identical chroma, one inherently light and one inherently dark. Take the four hundred most chromatic yellow pixels in this reproduction and the four hundred most chromatic blue ones: the yellows average chroma 65 at L* 70, the blues chroma 66 at L* 27. Same colour strength, forty-three points of lightness apart.
Squint until the brushwork blurs and you get the same answer without measuring — the stars survive as separate light notes while the sky sinks into one dark mass. Van Gogh neither lightened the yellow nor darkened the blue.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The colour wheel, and why there is more than one — Image Wiki
answer:
Harris, 1776: red sits opposite green
Munsell: red sits opposite blue-green


Left: Moses Harris, the "Prismatic" plate from The Natural System of Colours, 1776 — a hand-coloured engraving in 18 sectors, on cream paper with brown foxing across the blue and blue-purple sectors at left. Right: the Munsell hue-notation circle, after A. H. Munsell (1858–1918) — a line diagram, 40 spokes and a 100-step rim, with no colour on it at all. Both public domain. Read Harris for positions rather than exact hues; the pigments are 250 years old.
Read the labels and the two plates contradict each other. Harris puts RED at twelve o'clock and Green at six: red opposite green, orange opposite blue, yellow opposite purple. Look at his centre — three overlapping triangles, crimson, grey-blue and yellow, meeting in solid black. That is the red-yellow-blue claim, drawn.
Munsell puts R at twelve o'clock and BG at six, with N for neutral at the hub. Red is opposite blue-green, yellow opposite purple-blue, and green opposite red-purple. This is not a rounding difference. Harris's wheel records how paints were believed to mix; Munsell's is built from psychophysical measurement of how far apart people judge colour chips to look. One is a painter's object, the other a measurement notation — and the notation needs no ink to do its job.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The colour wheel, and why there is more than one — Image Wiki
answer:
M.-E. Chevreul, 1er cercle chromatique … renfermant les couleurs franches, plate engraved by Digeon and printed by Lemercier for J.-B. Baillière et Fils, Paris, 1864. Science History Institute via Wikimedia Commons; public domain.
Seventy-two hand-coloured sectors, each divided from the next by a hairline of bare paper, with named cartouches and numbered steps around the rim — industrial precision, ninety years after Harris. Find the names: VERT at the very top, ROUGE at the very bottom, JAUNE upper right, ORANGE lower right, VIOLET lower left, BLEU upper left.
Now follow the diameters. Rouge is still opposite vert, orange still opposite bleu, jaune still opposite violet. Ninety years of refinement inside the red-yellow-blue tradition did not move one cardinal point. So the disagreement in the pair above is not sloppiness on either side — it is two traditions answering two different questions, each self-consistent.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Colour management — Image Wiki
answer:
Robert Cooke, X-Rite ColorChecker Passport, 27 January 2013. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Profiling any device starts with measuring known colours: the ICC notes that "one of the first steps in profile building involves measuring a set of colors from some imaging media or display" (PRINT-004, §2). This is the camera version of that chart — the lower panel is the classic 24 patches, six of them a neutral grey ramp along the bottom row. Photograph it under the light you care about, compare what the camera recorded against the values the patches are known to have, and the difference is the profile.
For a press the same idea runs the other way: print a chart of hundreds of ink combinations, measure the paper with a spectrophotometer, and build the tables from the gap between what you asked for and what the ink did.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Complementary colours — Image Wiki
answer:
Restful: violet-blue against green, Irises, 1889
Hostile: red against green, The Zouave, 1888


Left: Vincent van Gogh, Irises, 1889, J. Paul Getty Museum. Right: Vincent van Gogh, The Zouave, 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam. Both public domain. One painter, one year apart, two complementary pairs.
Irises is violet-blue against green, and it settles. Nothing in it is very chromatic: the violet petals measure about chroma 38, the leaves 26, the yellow-green band at the top 39, and nothing exceeds 39. The green family covers roughly 37 per cent of the canvas to the blues' 23, and the two interleave as hundreds of leaf edges rather than meeting along one line.
The Zouave is red against green, and it will not settle. Follow the edge of the fez against the flat green wall. Sampled either side, the two are almost the same lightness — L* in the low twenties to low thirties on both — at almost the same chroma, 34 to 48. Equal value, equal strength, one hard boundary: neither colour can become the background, so the edge buzzes. The cap is about 5 per cent of the frame and it dominates a wall four times its size.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Complementary colours — Image Wiki
answer:
Decorative: yellow against blue, Café Terrace at Night, 1888
Stark: the same pair, The Sower, 1888


Vincent van Gogh, Café Terrace at Night (Kröller-Müller Museum) and The Sower (Kröller-Müller Museum), both 1888, both public domain. Now the pair is held constant — yellow against blue-violet in both — and only the handling changes.
In the Café Terrace the two are near-matched in strength: the awning and lit wall run about chroma 47, the night sky about 36, and the warm areas take 30 per cent of the canvas to the sky's 19. Read the cobbles: gold and blue strokes alternate all the way down, so the two hues are woven rather than opposed. Decorative, not tense.
In The Sower the same hue pair is unbalanced on purpose. The sky reaches chroma 60 while the ploughed field sits near 25, and the field is shattered into blue, lilac and orange flecks that average out. One side is loud and whole, the other quiet and broken. Stark, from the same two hues.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Contrast — Image Wiki
answer:
Two values and nothing between them: Vallotton, La Manifestation, 1893
Almost no value difference anywhere: Turner, Norham Castle, Sunrise, c. 1845


Félix Vallotton, La Manifestation (The Demonstration), 1893, woodcut (National Gallery of Art, CC0). J. M. W. Turner, Norham Castle, Sunrise, c. 1845 (Tate). Public domain.
Vallotton has exactly two values: black ink and cream paper. No greys, no modelling, no gradient anywhere. And nothing is unclear — you can read coats, a checked scarf, a dropped top hat, a bare shoulder, a crowd in flight. Contrast at its maximum needs no help from anything else.
Turner works at the other extreme. Sky, water, mist and stone all sit in the top third of the value scale; the castle is a soft blue-grey mass you have to hunt for, and the horizon is a guess. With value nearly switched off, the picture leans on the two axes it has left: the small cow at the front is the only strongly coloured thing in the frame, and the sun's glow is the only concentration of anything. Both hold, but only just — and both would vanish in a bad greyscale conversion.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Contrast — Image Wiki
answer:
Vincent van Gogh, The Night Café, September 1888 (Yale University Art Gallery). Public domain.
Van Gogh described this room to his brother as an attempt to say something with red and green, and the hue difference he built is about as large as paint allows: blood-red walls against a green ceiling and a green billiard table.
Now squint at it. Almost all of that difference disappears. The room collapses into a light floor, a darker everything-above, and four bright lamps — because the reds and the greens, however far apart in hue, sit close together in value. Ask where your eye actually goes: the lamps, then the pale figure by the table. Both are value events. The hue is doing the mood; the drawing is being done by four small patches of light.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Depth cues — Image Wiki
answer:
Pietro Perugino, Christ Handing the Keys to St Peter, Sistine Chapel, 1481–82, fresco. Public domain. Smarthistory uses this fresco to teach pictorial space.
Nearly every cue below is running here at once, and they all agree. Follow the joints in the paving away from you: they close together toward the temple's open doorway, and each transverse band of slabs is shallower than the one before. Then compare bodies. The apostles at the front fill about two-fifths of the panel's height; the figures across the middle of the square are a fifth of their height; the ones in the temple doorway a twelfth — and each group's feet sit higher in the frame than the last group's. Finally look past the arches to the hills: pale, flat, near the colour of the sky, while the foreground robes are at full strength.
Cover the hills with a thumb: still deep. Cover the paving instead: still deep. That redundancy is the argument.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Depth cues — Image Wiki
answer:
Andrea Mantegna, Lamentation over the Dead Christ, c. 1470–74, Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan. Public domain.
Foreshortening at the limit. Compare one sole with the face above it: drawn at nearly the same size, absurd as a measurement and correct as a projection, because the feet are the nearest thing here and the head the furthest. Then measure with your fingers — his legs, over half his real length, take up no more picture height than his chest and belly.
Note what did not change: the thighs are full width. A form aimed at you keeps its width and loses its length. That is the difference between foreshortened and simply small.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Depth cues — Image Wiki
answer:
Serife Gerenschier, forced perspective at the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, Istanbul, 2017. CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons.
She stands a couple of metres from the lens; the mosque is much further. Her outline runs unbroken across the domes, the arches and the wall — that is overlap, and overlap almost never loses. Relative size is the cue that gives way, and your eye does not discard it, it rewrites it: she must be several storeys tall. The visitors by the doors are the scale that got overruled: roughly her height in reality, an eighth of it here.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Depth of field — Image Wiki
answer:
f/1.4
f/4
f/22


Alex1ruff, 2014. Five stacks of letter blocks receding from the camera, focus held on the front stack; only the aperture changed. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
At f/1.4 the front stack is crisp, the second is already soft and the fifth has dissolved into coloured shapes. At f/4 three stacks are readable. At f/22 all five are, down to the small "3" on the back block.
Watch the rate, not just the extent: at f/1.4 each stack is markedly softer than the one in front of it, a steep and continuous falloff along the receding line. That is what real optics does, and what blur painted on afterwards usually gets wrong.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Depth of field — Image Wiki
answer:
Kjoonlee, 2026, Heptagonal bokeh. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
Find the pale gaps of sky in the upper right, just past the leaves. They are not soft round blobs: each has straight sides and sharp corners, and the clearest are unambiguously seven-sided — the outline of the diaphragm, stamped on the image once per out-of-focus highlight. Below them, just right of the trunk, a lone turquoise highlight comes out as the same seven-sided shape in a different colour: the giveaway that the shape belongs to the lens, not to anything in the scene. Meanwhile the trunk and the nearest leaf edges are sharp enough to count veins.
Calling bokeh good or bad is taste; calling it heptagonal is fact.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Design tokens — Image Wiki
answer:
Specified: 1927
Built: Georgia, 2013


Left: Plate II of the AASHO Manual and Specifications for U.S. Standard Road Markers and Signs, 1927 (public domain). Right: a signpost in Georgia, photographed in 2013 by Dougtone (CC BY-SA 2.0).
Left, four designs, each with a code printed under it: M-4 the small directional shield, M-19 the arrow, M-19A the double arrow, D-4 the junction plate. The accompanying text is a specification, not advice: the route marker "is a shield bearing the name of the State, the number of the route and the letters 'U.S.'", and "the background color of the shield is white and the design black" (AASHO-1927).
Right, eighty-six years later, on a roadside in Georgia. The shield, the black-on-white scheme and the plain arrow plaque are all still there, on a post assembled by somebody who never read the manual. The decision outlived the committee, the drawing and the technology — which is the only test of a system that matters.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Design tokens — Image Wiki
answer:
Plate XXI, Caution Series, AASHO 1927. Public domain.
This is what "a limited set of discrete options" looks like on paper. Six diamonds, and every one has a number: C-1 is HILL, C-2 is HILL SHIFT GEAR, C-3 is CURVE, and so on. A county engineer does not design a warning sign. They pick one, by number, from a list.
The list is also revealing about what a system is for. When a state needed something new, the manual says the design would be worked out with them and "thereafter be included in the list, and any other State wishing a sign for the same purpose will find it provided among the Standards" (AASHO-1927). A contribution process, in 1927, in one sentence.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Naming what is wrong — Image Wiki
answer:
Walker Evans, Bud Fields and his family at home, Hale County, Alabama, 1936. Library of Congress, public domain.
Worth running the checklist on a photograph that passes, so you know what agreement looks like. The window at the right edge is blown white, and the floorboards get steadily darker as they run away from it — one source, and the falloff proves where it is. Every bare foot and every chair leg has a small, tight, dark seam where it meets the floor: nobody is hovering. The floorboards and the wall boards converge consistently, and everyone's eye level sits at the same height, which is what tells you the camera was low, at about the height of a seated adult.
None of that is what the picture is about. It is the substrate that lets you believe the room exists.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Naming what is wrong — Image Wiki
answer:
Marion Post Wolcott, Negro man entering movie theatre by the "colored" entrance, Belzoni, Mississippi, October 1939. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Two unrelated shadows, one answer. The stairway's canopy throws a big wedge of dark across the brick, down and to the right of its own edge; the folding ladder standing against the white wall throws a smaller one in the same direction, at the same slant. Sun high and to our left, and only one of it. Both edges are hard lines you could trace with a pencil, which is the second agreement: one small source, so nothing in the frame is allowed a soft edge.
Then use the ladder for step 2. Its shadow does not touch it — the dark shape sits well to the right of the real ladder, and that gap measures how far the ladder stands off the wall. An object flush against a surface has its shadow welded to it; an offset shadow means air behind. Either can be right, but the offset and the distance have to agree.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Naming what is wrong — Image Wiki
answer:
Willem Kalf, Still Life with a Silver Jug and a Porcelain Bowl, c. 1656. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
The silver jug has almost no colour of its own. Read its surface and you are reading the room: black patches where it reflects the dark niche, a pale streak up its left flank, and a broad warm gold wash across its belly picked up from the gilt cup and the fruit standing beside it. Cover the neighbours and most of the jug's tone has no source. That is the test for metal — its shading is a distorted picture of what surrounds it, not a smooth ramp from light to dark.
Now the lemon in front. Its sheen is a pale, near-white bloom lying on top of the yellow, not a more intense yellow: a non-metal returns the light's own colour and keeps its body colour underneath. The porcelain bowl does the same along its rim. And look where the jug's foot and the lemon meet the ledge — a dark, tight seam under each, which is step 2 passing.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Naming what is wrong — Image Wiki
answer:
Eugène Atget, Rue Saint-Rustique, Montmartre, Paris, March 1922. Museum of Modern Art. Public domain.
Three checks on one street. The kerb, the gutter and the base of the right-hand wall all run to the same small area at the top of the slope: one set of parallel lines, one meeting point. The cobbles do the other half of the job — each stone is a known size, and they shrink and flatten steadily instead of in jumps, so distance and size stay in step the whole way up.
The subtlety is worth having. Because the street climbs, the point those lines meet at sits above your eye level rather than on the horizon. A slope does not break the rule, it moves the target — which is why "the lines meet somewhere sensible" is a stronger check than "the lines meet on the horizon".

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Diffuse and specular — Image Wiki
answer:
Figure by Scratchapixel, What is Shading: Light-Matter interaction, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
Compare the two bundles of arrows. Going in, on the right, red, green and blue are the same thickness — white light. Coming out, on the left, red and green are unchanged and the blue has been reduced to a hairline: the skin absorbed it. Red plus green added as light is the orange disc at the top left.
So the colour of an object is not something its surface adds. It is what is left of the lamp's light after the material has taken its cut, and it can only exist on this route — the arrows go in and out of the same patch of skin rather than bouncing off the top of it. Which is also why the highlight beside it is white: that light never went in, so nothing filtered it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Diffuse and specular — Image Wiki
answer:
Figure by Scratchapixel, Reflection, Refraction and Fresnel, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
Sunlight on rippled water: the specular route run a few thousand times at once, with the result of each test visible separately. Every white star is one patch of surface tilted so that its mirror direction happens to point at the camera. The plain dark blue between the stars is the same water under the same sun, failing that test by a degree or two.
Nothing in the pattern belongs to the water. Move the camera and a different set of patches lights up; hold still and the ripples travel, so it reshuffles anyway. And every glint is the same colour — white, the sun's, not the sea's — because each one is a small picture of the source.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Diffuse and specular — Image Wiki
answer:
Stuart Kerr, Multi Colour Pool Balls in Triangle, 2009. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Fifteen different diffuse colours; fifteen identical white specular highlights, each in the same place on its ball. The orange 5, the yellow 9 and the green 14 agree about nothing except their highlights — because the highlight belongs to the lamp, not to the ball. Each is a hard-edged little rectangle with a smaller glint beside it, repeated identically fifteen times: two rectangular sources somewhere above the table. Cross-check that against the shadows, as in Hard and soft light. The red cloth is close to pure diffuse — not a glint anywhere on it, just its own colour.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Diffuse and specular — Image Wiki
answer:
Almost all diffuse: Sánchez Cotán, c. 1602
Specular does the work: Kalf, 1656


Two still lifes lit the same way — one strong source from the left, a dark surround — sorted by which route dominates.
Sánchez Cotán chose objects that are nearly all diffuse: quince skin, cabbage leaf, cut melon, dressed stone. Track the melon — brightest where it faces the light, darkening smoothly round the curve, and nowhere a bright spot of a different colour from the melon. The one glossy object is the cucumber, and it carries the picture's only real highlight.
Kalf chose the opposite. On the silver ewer the diffuse route is gone entirely (see Metal and everything else) and what is left is a contorted picture of the room. On the lemons both routes run at once: hold on the front one and you get yellow body colour with a scatter of tiny white pinpricks over the pitted skin, in the colour of the light, not of the lemon.
Juan Sánchez Cotán, Still Life with Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber, c. 1602, and Willem Kalf, Still Life with a Silver Jug and a Porcelain Bowl, 1656. Both public domain.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Edges and merges — Image Wiki
answer:
Diego Velázquez, Juan de Pareja, 1650 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
All three edge qualities in one head, and you can find each of them in about five seconds.
Hard: the white collar against the dark doublet. A traceable zigzag, the crispest boundary in the painting, and it sits directly under the face — which is where Velázquez wanted you.
Soft: the top and right of the hair against the grey wall. There is a boundary, but it takes a finger's width to happen, and if you try to say exactly where the hair ends you cannot.
Lost: the lower left. His shoulder and cloak are the same value as the ground behind them and the contour is simply absent — the figure has no left-hand outline below the shoulder at all. Nothing is wrong with the picture. The edges that survived are the ones that describe the face, and the ones that were given up were describing a sleeve.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Edges and merges — Image Wiki
answer:
The full frame: a loaded truck, three men, a boy climbing, a utility pole
Our own detail of the three men against the cab


Jack Delano, French-Canadian potato farmers near Caribou, Maine, October 1940. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress; public domain. The right panel is our own crop of the left one.
A real photograph, by a very good photographer, with real merges in it — the ordinary kind rather than the cartoon kind.
In the detail, find the outline of the man in the middle. Down his right side, around his raised arm and over his shoulder there is nothing to find: his dark jacket and the truck's dark cab are the same value and the boundary between them does not exist. What rescues him is three small hard edges — the pale glove up at the wing mirror, the checked shirt, the light collar. Cover those with a fingertip and he loses his shape. The seated man on the right is in the same position: his shoulder merges into the cab, and his pale hat is doing all the separating.
In the full frame, look at the utility pole on the right. Its foot disappears behind the boy climbing the tailboard, so pole and boy read as one dark upright, and the pole then runs off the top edge and takes the eye with it. That is the tangent the textbooks describe, found in the wild rather than staged.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Exposure and dynamic range — Image Wiki
answer:
Exposed for the view out of the window
Exposed for the room, several stops brighter


Axel Jacobs, 2006, two frames from one bracketed set: same room, same window, same time of day, only the exposure changed. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
Left: the view records properly — separate leaves, power lines against blue sky, an iron fence, coloured marbles on the sill. Indoors is gone: the dressmaker's dummy is a flat silhouette, the armchair a shape you could not identify.
Right: the room records properly — cream walls, dado rail, floorboards, a red chair with a yellow cushion. Now look back at the window: one flat white panel with a ghost of foliage low in the glass. The power lines, the sky and the fence are not in the file.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Exposure and dynamic range — Image Wiki
answer:
Daniel Schwen, 2003. The same frame twice: below, every pixel sitting at pure white has been repainted red. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5.
Look at the steel table plate across the bottom. Its left half is full of information — scratches, punch marks, a dent, the grain of the metal. Its right half, where the sun lands, is one continuous red field: same plate, same material, no surface recorded at all. In the upper picture that passes for an ordinary highlight on metal.
The daylight behind the men is solid red too, with no gradient in it. The pale jacket is stippled red across the shoulder — half the pixels at the limit, half just under — which is what a surface sitting right on the edge of the range looks like. Everything unmarked still holds tone, the near-black cast iron of the press included.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Focal length vs camera position — Image Wiki
answer:
Close, wide lens: 17 mm
Far, long lens: 200 mm


Armin Kübelbeck, 2008, from a series at seven focal lengths with the subject held the same size in the frame. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Her head is about the same width in both. Now compare the feet, the nearest thing to the camera. At 17 mm one foot is wider than her head and the legs run away down a long stretch of jeans; at 200 mm a foot is about as wide as her head, and the legs have collapsed to almost nothing.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Focal length vs camera position — Image Wiki
answer:
24 mm, close to the subject
400 mm, far from the subject


Florian Schott, 2007, same footbridge, same f/5.6, subject held the same size in the frame. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Follow the handrail she is leaning on. At 24 mm it runs away down the bridge deck to a vanishing point and brings the whole gorge with it: conifers on the far side drawn small, the rock face beyond them smaller still. At 400 mm that handrail crosses the lower frame almost flat, and the rock face — which never moved — fills the whole background and reads as a wall close behind her.
She is the same size in both, so it is the background magnification that changed. The softer rendering on the right is a second consequence of shooting from far back with a long lens; see Depth of field.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Framing and cropping — Image Wiki
answer:
The frame as Vachon made it: two girls, a mailbox, a rolled newspaper
Our own tight crop of the same negative


John Vachon, Ozark children getting mail from RFD box, Missouri, May 1940. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress; public domain. The right panel is our own crop of the left one; nothing else was changed.
Left is about the mail. The open box, the rolled newspaper in her raised hand, the row of neighbours' boxes cut off by the top edge, the second child watching from behind her shoulder — every one of those is a decision to keep something.
Right is a good portrait of a girl, and it is not a better or a worse picture. It is a different one. The box, the newspaper and the errand are gone; so is the second child, and so is the reason the first one is smiling at somebody. Cropping tighter always improves something — here it removes two real competitors for attention — and the bill is paid in subject matter.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Framing and cropping — Image Wiki
answer:
Pieter de Hooch, The Courtyard of a House in Delft, 1658 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
Count the frames. The painting's own edge; then the brick arch on the left with its dated tablet above it; then, deep in the passage, a second arch; then the bright window at the end of it. Four rectangles nested inside one another, and that nesting alone builds the depth — no perspective trickery required, just one shape overlapping the next, which is the most basic depth device there is (POST-001-SUP1).
Look at what the arch buys for the woman standing in the passage. She is small, she is turned away, her dark bodice barely separates from the wall — and you find her instantly, because she is the only thing inside an enclosure and she has the frame's brightest patch directly behind her.
Then look at the cost, because it is real. The arch is a wall as well as a window: your eye goes into it, arrives at the far window, and has to be dragged back out to the woman and child on the right. The picture is two compartments rather than one room.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Framing and cropping — Image Wiki
answer:
Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877 (Art Institute of Chicago). Public domain.
The decisive cut, made on purpose by a painter who could have put the border anywhere he liked. At the right edge a man in a top hat is sliced from crown to boots — roughly half of him, umbrella included, is outside the picture. Nobody reads that as a mistake. It reads as a street that carries on past the canvas, and the pedestrian traffic in the frame becomes a sample of something larger.
Compare it with the near-miss he avoided. Had that man been shifted a hand's width to the left, with only a shoulder and a sliver of hat clipped off, the eye would go straight to the damage. Cut a lot or cut nothing.
Note the lamp post while you are here: a hard vertical almost exactly on the centre line, dividing the canvas into a near half and a far half. A frame does not only have four edges; anything running from top to bottom acts as one.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Roughness and Fresnel — Image Wiki
answer:
Figure by Scratchapixel, What is Shading: Light-Matter interaction, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
The yellow rays arrive parallel, as they would from one small lamp. The purple rays are what leaves. Each purple ray is a full-strength mirror bounce — the facet it met obeyed angle-in-equals-angle-out exactly — but because neighbouring facets are tilted differently, no two leave in the same direction. In the lower panel the surface is rougher and the fan is wider still.
Nothing in either panel absorbs anything: the same light leaves, aimed differently. That is the microfacet claim in its rawest form, and it is what the four spheres below say again in brightness curves.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Roughness and Fresnel — Image Wiki
answer:
Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), Distorting water reflections at Digermulen port, Hinnøya, Norway, September 2015. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
One surface, one scene, one light — and two roughnesses in the same frame, because a passing boat has roughened half of it. Along the top and behind the boat the water is glass-smooth: the rocks, the grass and the waterline come back as a legible second copy of the shore. In the lower two-thirds the wake has tilted the surface into slow ripples, and the same shore is stretched into unrecognisable bands of green and white — but not into anything dimmer. Only the organisation is gone. Scratchapixel makes this point with a lightly rippled lake: wind does at centimetre scale what microscopic roughness does at micron scale (SRC-093).

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Roughness and Fresnel — Image Wiki
answer:
Figure by Scratchapixel, Reflection, Refraction and Fresnel, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
One flat surface, one photograph, and the whole curve laid out by distance. The red lines are sight lines across the water, all converging on the horizon: at the bottom of the frame you are looking steeply down into it, and by the far shore your line of sight has flattened almost along it. Where it is steep, transmission wins and you read the lake bed pebble by pebble. Where it flattens — the strip just under the horizon — reflection wins, and the water hands back a featureless pale sheet of sky instead. The pebbles are still down there. Nothing hides them but the angle, which is the left-hand curve above walked from 0° at your feet to nearly 90° at the far shore (SRC-094).

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Roughness and Fresnel — Image Wiki
answer:
Mikhail Kim, Barclays Center Rain Night, 2012. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
The same walk up the frame, on tarmac instead of water, and the road is equally wet from end to end. Near the bottom you can still read the surface itself: asphalt grain, yellow lane lines, the white "ONLY" lettering. Further away the road stops being a road and becomes a mirror — signage, street lamps and lit facade all stretched into long streaks running toward you.
The streaks are long for a second reason: this is Fresnel and roughness at once, each source smeared along the direction the ripples tilt, as in the harbour photograph above. A still film of water would give short sharp inverted copies instead.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Gestalt grouping — Image Wiki
answer:
Meindert Hobbema, The Avenue at Middelharnis, 1689 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
Continuity in a real picture, and the reason it is worth a figure: watch where your eye goes without being asked. It starts at the bottom edge, picks up one of the wheel ruts, and runs up the track to the tiny walking figure and the church tower beyond.
Nothing forces that. The ruts are broken, puddled and interrupted, and the trunks cut across them; your visual system stitches the fragments into one continuous line and then follows it. That is also why a road, a fence, a handrail or a shoreline will hijack a composition whether or not it points at the subject.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Gestalt grouping — Image Wiki
answer:
Large-tailed nightjar (Caprimulgus macrurus) roosting, Bharatpur, 2015. Photograph by Tanmay Haldar via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
There is a bird in the left half of this picture, lying along the branch. It takes most people a few seconds, and this is what a merger looks like when nature does it on purpose.
Work out what is missing. The bird's outline is all there — you can trace head, shoulder, folded wing and tail. But every cue that would separate it from the branch is absent: the same browns, the same mid-tones, the same streaky bark-like texture, and no shadow gap under the body because it is pressed flat to the wood. Similarity groups the bird with the branch, so there is no second object for your eye to find.
Two things do eventually give it away, and both are local breaks in the pattern: the dark slit of the closed eye, and a short crisp edge where the folded wing overlaps the bark near the bottom left. A merger in a photograph fails or succeeds on exactly these — not on how "cluttered" the background looks.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Grids — Image Wiki
answer:
A page from the Gutenberg Bible, about 1455, in the Library of Congress copy (this one hand-illuminated after printing). Public domain.
Every part of the diagram above is here, 570 years before anyone said "grid system". Two columns with a narrow gutter you could not fit a finger into. A fixed line count per column, so both columns end level. Margins so generous that the text occupies little more than half the sheet, one side margin visibly wider than the other, and a bottom margin about twice the top.
Look at the right edge of each column: the lines end flush, held there by abbreviations and varying word space. That flushness is not decoration — it is what makes the column read as a rectangle, which is what lets the eye find the next line without hunting. And note the illuminated vine, which ignores the grid completely. A grid governs the structural elements. It does not forbid anything else.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Grids — Image Wiki
answer:
The New York Times, front page, 16 April 1912. Public domain.
Eight columns, one fixed gutter, one measure for every line of body text on the sheet. The banner headline spans all eight; the photograph spans four and stops exactly on a column boundary; the stacked one-column decks down the left and right edges are all the same width because there is only one width available. Even the ruled lines that separate stories sit on column boundaries.
Nothing here is spare, quiet or geometric in the Swiss sense. It is grey, cramped and ornamental at the masthead. It is also more strictly gridded than most modernist posters, and it had to be: the grid is what let a dozen people set type in parallel overnight and have it fit.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How images mean — Image Wiki
answer:
E. J. Kealey, Women of Britain Say — "Go!", Parliamentary Recruiting Committee, London, May 1915. Public domain.
Denotation first, and only denotation: three people at an open casement, five soldiers with packs and rifles on a road beyond a low wall, a hill with one tree, a ploughed brown field in front.
Now the second layer, which is not in the paint. The window frame puts the women indoors and the men outdoors, so the picture is about leaving. The woman in front holds the other's arm and neither looks at the boy; the boy holds on to her shawl. The ring on the hand resting on that arm tells you she has a husband, and the picture does not show him — his absence is the argument. None of that is depicted. All of it is read.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How images mean — Image Wiki
answer:
The Pioneer 10 plaque, NASA, 1972; designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake, artwork by Linda Salzman Sagan. Public domain (NASA).
Gombrich's list of what a finder would have to know already. That some lines are outlines and others are shading — nothing in the engraving says which. That the raised right hand means greeting; he notes that a Chinese or Indian viewer could not read that gesture from their own repertoire either. That the arrowhead on the trajectory at the bottom means direction of travel, which requires a species that once had bows and arrows. That the two separate diagrams are separate diagrams.
Every one of those is a convention. A code is a set of them, shared by a group, and a sign only means anything inside one. Photography is no exception: it had to be learned before it became invisible, and the first instant snapshots confused Western viewers who had never seen movement stopped.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How images mean — Image Wiki
answer:
High modality: a photograph, with everything the lens happened to include
Lower modality: a plate, with nothing in it that was not chosen


The same bird, Phoenicopterus ruber. Left: photograph by Cliff (Arlington, Virginia), 2007, CC BY 2.0. Right: Robert Havell after John James Audubon, American Flamingo, 1838, National Gallery of Art, CC0.
Left says "I was standing there". The evidence is all the stuff nobody chose: a palm trunk sliced off by the frame edge, feathers dropped on mown grass, a wandering ibis, an artificial pond lip.
Right claims nothing of the kind, and tells you so in three places. The bird is bent double because the paper ended, not because flamingos fold like that. Dissections of the bill, tongue and foot float in the top margin at a different scale, in a different technique. The background flock is drawn at a wholly different scale from the foreground bird. This is a specimen record, and it is more accurate than the photograph about the bill.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How images mean — Image Wiki
answer:
Cornelis Norbertus Gijsbrechts, Trompe l'oeil. The Reverse of a Framed Painting, 1668–72, Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen. Public domain.
A painting whose entire subject is a modality claim. There is no scene: the canvas shows the back of a canvas — bare weave, the stretcher, the tack heads, a curling paper label with a number on it. Every high-modality cue Chandler lists is loaded on purpose, and the picture uses them to say "I am not a picture, I am an object in your room."
Look for the same cues doing the same job in a render that wants to pass as a photograph: dust, fingerprints, chromatic fringing, a slightly wrong crop.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to look at an image — Image Wiki
answer:
Rothstein's dust storm as photographed
The same file blurred by us, standing in for a squint


Arthur Rothstein, Dust storm, Cimarron County, Oklahoma, April 1936. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain. The right panel is our own blur of the left one.
Squinting, done arithmetically. Everything on the right collapses into four things: a pale sky, a mid-grey ground, one dark horizontal mass — the shed — and two small dark accents. Nothing else in the frame survives: the corrugated iron, the boards, the fence wire were detail sitting on a structure that works without them.
One thing the blur reveals that the sharp version hides. There are three people on the left panel, but only two dark accents on the right: the boy walking behind the man has merged into him. At squint size they are a single shape, and that is how the photograph actually reads.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to look at an image — Image Wiki
answer:
Eugène Atget, Boucherie, Rue Christine, Paris, between 1895 and 1927. Library of Congress. Public domain.
The subject is a butcher's window. Nothing is beautiful and nothing is happening. Now describe the construction instead: one bright shape — the hanging meat and the marble sill — held inside a much darker frame of stone and shuttered wood, with the open doorway to its left as the deepest black in the picture. The only other light anywhere is the strip of pavement along the bottom edge, and it is kept flat and empty.
That is why a photograph of nothing holds together, and it is the whole argument against judging an image by what it is a picture of.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to look at an image — Image Wiki
answer:
Dorothea Lange, Migrant Mother, Nipomo, California, 1936. Library of Congress, public domain.
Steps 1 and 2 on one frame. Where did you land? Her face — and squinting shows why. The tent, the clothes and the children all collapse into one mid-grey, and the only light shape left is her forehead, cheek and hand, which is also the only sharply detailed area in the picture. That is not luck: both older children have turned their faces into her shoulders, so there is no second face to compete, and the baby is a pale blur at the bottom edge.
Step 3 falls out of the same look. Her nose casts a small shadow straight down rather than across a cheek and the transitions across her face are gradual, so the light is soft, frontal and from above.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: How to look at an image — Image Wiki
answer:
Jack Delano, Chicago, Illinois. In the waiting room of Union Station, January 1943. Office of War Information, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Step 3 is usually detective work; here the evidence is lying in the open. The clerestory windows are in the top of the frame, and every beam leaves them heading down and to the right at the same angle — one source, high and to our left. Check that against the floor: the bright pools land to the lower right of the windows that made them, and where a body interrupts a beam the floor behind it stays dark.
Then do step 4 on the same picture. Your eye entered at the windows, slid down a beam and stopped on the two policemen — the darkest shapes standing in the brightest patch in the frame. The rays are not decoration, they are the path.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Icon, pictogram, symbol, glyph, logo — Image Wiki
answer:
Photo: Glogger, Washroom pictogram sign with braille, 2008, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Four of the five categories on one plate. The man and the woman are pictograms — pictures of the expected occupants. The wheelchair is the International Symbol of Accessibility, a symbol: it does not mean "wheelchairs", it means "accessible", and you had to be told. WASHROOM is set in glyphs. The braille strip is a fifth writing system that is not required to contrast with the plate, because fingers do not care about contrast.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Identity systems — Image Wiki
answer:
NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.1 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
Read the last paragraph. The logotype "must not be re-drawn, but rather reproduced photographically from reproduction artwork included in Section 2 of this manual." In 1976 that instruction was the entire version-control system: Section 2 of the binder holds camera-ready sheets of the mark and the signatures, and a print shop shot them with a camera rather than tracing them.
The reason is in the drawing above it. All four letters are one stroke width, and the cross-strokes are gone from both A's. Any of that redrawn by hand comes back slightly wrong, and slightly wrong, repeated across an agency for a decade, is a different mark.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Identity systems — Image Wiki
answer:
NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.7 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
For large applications such as signage the mark may be rebuilt, but only from this grid, and the manual pins the scale with one number: three grid units equal the vertical stroke width. Count the squares across the upright of the N and you will find three.
That single ratio turns an aesthetic judgement into arithmetic a sign fabricator can execute in a workshop, without the manual, without a designer on the phone. It is also why the page is turned on its side and is mostly grid: the drawing is a tool, not an illustration.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Identity systems — Image Wiki
answer:
Section 5.3: the specified typeface
Section 5.14: the grid method


NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, pp. 5.3 and 5.14 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
Left: Helvetica, named as "the most important family of type in the NASA Unified Visual Communications System" — Light for text and for the agency name locked to the logotype, Medium for headings. Below the alphabets are the same paragraph set two ways, which is how you check a specification rather than admire it.
Right: the grid, in three steps. Blank spread, then the two-column structure that fixes every margin, gutter and page number, then the same spread with headline, columns, a photograph and captions dropped into it. The manual's own reason for the grid is not beauty: it "will save countless man hours in execution."

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The ethics of making and choosing images — Image Wiki
answer:
As Gardner titled it: "A Sharpshooter's Last Sleep"
The same man, retitled: "Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter"


Alexander Gardner, Gettysburg, July 1863; both plates appear in Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the War, 1866. Library of Congress and National Archives; both public domain.
One dead man, twice. Follow the dark coat, the white cloth bunched at the chest and the head thrown back with the mouth open across both frames. On the left he lies in open ground with a rifle laid flat in front of him. On the right he is tucked into a stone barricade in Devil's Den, and a musket now stands propped against the rock — the tidy vertical that makes the composition work.
Gardner's crew carried the body about forty yards between exposures. Every grain of both negatives is a true record of light. The second title claims he was a sharpshooter, shot at his own post, and the negative cannot support that.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The ethics of making and choosing images — Image Wiki
answer:
Wide: pebbles, a dry stem at the bottom edge, ground with texture
Tight: nothing in the frame but cracks


Arthur Rothstein, a steer skull in the South Dakota badlands, 1936, made for the US Resettlement Administration. Library of Congress; public domain.
The same skull, the same afternoon, two exposures — and it has been picked up and turned between them, which is why the story broke when a newspaper noticed. Look only at what the frame decides. Left, loose pebbles, a change of surface across the top, a dry stem at the bottom edge. Right, cracked alkali to every edge, and the drought is total.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The ethics of making and choosing images — Image Wiki
answer:
Jacob Riis, Lodgers in a Crowded Bayard Street Tenement, New York, c. 1889, from How the Other Half Lives. Public domain.
Riis went into lodging rooms at night and fired magnesium flash powder. The evidence is in the faces: the man in the upper bunk, propped on one elbow, looking straight down the lens with the expression of somebody who has just been woken by an explosion; the two heads at the right, half out of the blankets. They are barefoot, in bed, in a room the size of a cupboard, and they are identifiable.
The photographs helped force New York to change its housing law. Both things are true at once, and pretending otherwise is the easy way out.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Legibility and readability — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "Introducing accessibility in typography". Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
Two different measurements in one picture. Top row is legibility, and it is decided glyph by glyph: on the left the vertical strokes are interchangeable, on the right the 1 has a flag and the I has crossbars, so you can name each one on sight.
Bottom row is readability, and it is decided by the setting rather than the drawing. Both paragraphs are the same typeface. The left one is set larger against a fixed line height, so the lines are jammed together and the descenders push into the row below; the right one is smaller and breathes. Nothing about the letterforms changed.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Legibility and readability — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "Introducing accessibility in typography" — the typefaces Andika, Lexend and Atkinson Hyperlegible. Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
Three faces drawn specifically to keep these pairs apart. Look at the third column: the zero has a slash through it, the l has a tail, the 1 has both a flag and a foot. Each of those is a deliberate structural tell, not a flourish.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Legibility and readability — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "Introducing accessibility in typography". Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
The tinted shapes are the counters; the leader lines mark where each letter opens. Left, the openings are nearly shut, so a c at small size fills in and becomes an o, and an e becomes a c. Right, the same three letters with the openings held wide — Google Fonts notes that more white inside a letter also makes it look larger, which is a second, free benefit.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light direction — Image Wiki
answer:
Figure by Scratchapixel, Diffuse and Lambertian Shading, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
One beam of light, same width and same power in all three positions; only the angle at which it meets the grey plane changes. On the left it stands square-on and its footprint is the size of the beam itself. In the middle it is tilted, and the footprint has grown: the yellow core is the patch of surface (dA), the green fringe is the extra floor the tilt added, and the whole ellipse is the beam's oblique footprint (dL). Brightness is the ratio of the two — dA over dL (SRC-095) — so it drops as the fringe grows. On the right the beam is nearly flat along the plane and has almost stopped landing on it at all.
The numbers above are that ratio. Nothing is absorbed anywhere in the series: the shaded side of every ball, every apple and every cheek is dark purely because the same light was made to cover more surface.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light direction — Image Wiki
answer:
Walker Evans, Allie Mae Burroughs, Hale County, Alabama, 1936. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. Public domain.
This is what a light beside the lens does. Hunt for a shadow and you will find almost nothing to hold: a short one under the nose, a thin one under the chin and the lower lip, a faint darkening where the neck meets the collar. The clapboard wall behind her — the one surface in frame that could receive a cast shadow — carries none, so the light was close to the axis the camera is looking down.
Every surface the camera can see is a surface the light can see, so the shadows hide directly behind the things casting them. Notice what survives and what does not: the texture of the boards and the freckles is fully described, and the form of the head is not. Cheekbones, brow and jaw are stated by their outlines and by tone changes in the skin, not by shading. It is a portrait of a surface.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light direction — Image Wiki
answer:
Alfred T. Palmer, Operating a hand drill at Vultee-Nashville, Tennessee, February 1943. Library of Congress FSA/OWI Collection. Public domain.
Compare this with the Evans portrait: one light, moved off the axis. Start where the checklist below starts. There is a cast shadow here — the head's, thrown onto the yellow panel behind and to her right, with an edge you can trace — so the source sits out of frame to the camera's left, at about head height, and it is small enough to draw a hard edge.
Now look at what that bought. The eye socket is a distinct pocket of shade under a lit brow; there is a shadow beside the nose and another under the cheekbone; the far side of the jaw goes down into halftone while the front of the face stays lit. Every one of those is a piece of the face turned away from a light that is off to one side — the shaded fraction the frontal portrait had none of, and the reason the head reads as a solid object rather than a surface.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light direction — Image Wiki
answer:
Gerrit van Honthorst, A Boy Blowing on a Firebrand, 1621–22 (Art Institute of Chicago). Public domain.
The source is in the picture, held below his chin, and everything follows from that position. Work upward from the firebrand: the underside of the nose is the brightest part of the face, the upper lip and the shelf of the chin catch light, and the shadow of the nose runs up onto the cheek instead of down. His brow is lit from beneath, so the ridge that normally shades the eyes is now shading the forehead above them.
The plume in his hat settles it: it is lit along its lower edges and dark on top. This is the direction that reads as sinister when nothing explains it, and here it reads as an ordinary boy with an ordinary ember, because the ember is in frame doing the work.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light falloff — Image Wiki
answer:
Georges de La Tour, The Magdalen with the Smoking Flame, c. 1640. One candle, and it is close — so this is falloff at its most extreme. Public domain.
Follow the light outward from the flame. The books and the skull sitting beside it are blazing. Her hands, maybe twice as far, are already dimmer. Her shoulder and the folds of the sleeve behind it drop further again, and the wall a metre back is simply gone. Nothing here is painted black because it is a dark object; the wall is presumably an ordinary wall. It is dark because it is far from a small flame.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light falloff — Image Wiki
answer:
Joseph Wright of Derby, A Philosopher Giving that Lecture on the Orrery, in which a Lamp is put in place of the Sun, c. 1766 (Derby Museum and Art Gallery). Public domain.
The single source is the lamp standing in for the sun inside the machine, hidden behind the silhouetted boy at the centre. It is a distance ladder, and you can rank four rungs of it by eye alone.
Start at the two children leaning over the brass rings: nearest the lamp, and so bright their cheeks are near white. Step back to the lecturer in the red robe, further out and clearly duller though he faces the lamp squarely. Step back again to the man taking notes at the left, dimmer still. Then the bookcase in the top right corner, where a few spines catch just enough to be legible.
Nothing in that sequence is a darker object than the one before it. The only thing that changed along the way is distance — and this is the same fact the diagram states as a curve, with the lamp deliberately hidden so that only its effect is visible.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light falloff — Image Wiki
answer:
Alfred T. Palmer, riveter at the Vultee-Nashville aircraft plant, Tennessee, February 1943. Library of Congress FSA/OWI Collection. Public domain.
The photograph the paragraph above describes, taken in a factory. She and the aluminium panel under her hands are fully exposed; two metres past her the building has gone black.
The important part is what is in that black. Look along the left edge and at the top: an air hose, a chain, some framing, faintly legible. The space is there and it is an ordinary lit factory — it is simply much further from the lamp than she is, so it lands four or five stops down and photographs as nothing. A dark background tells you very little about the room a photograph was taken in.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Light falloff — Image Wiki
answer:
John Constable, The Hay Wain, 1821 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
The same law, read from the flat end. Pick the sunlit grass on the near bank, then the sunlit meadow beyond the trees, then the field at the horizon perhaps half a mile away. They are the same brightness, and the pale figures out in that far meadow on the right are lit as strongly as the cart standing in the foreground water.
