The source here is the sun and the whole sky, and nothing in the scene is measurably closer to either. Distance in this picture is carried by haze, by detail and by colour — never by dimming, because there is no dimming available. A lamp would have run out of light before the second tree.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Hard and soft light — Image Wiki
answer:
Hard: direct sun, June 1939
Soft: heavy overcast, November 1940


Left: Marion Post Wolcott, church in a corn field, Manning, South Carolina, June 1939. Right: Jack Delano, A square with old houses in an old fishing village, Stonington, Conn., November 1940. Both Library of Congress FSA/OWI Kodachromes, catalogued under their original titles; both public domain.
Same planet, same star, two Kodachrome frames of a wooden building. Left, the sun: half a degree wide, so every solid thing draws a shadow you could trace. The eaves lay a hard-edged band of shade across the boards below them, the tree is a single dark mass, and each corn leaf casts its own little shadow — which is why the field reads as crunchy texture rather than green paint.
Right, the same sun behind a cloud deck. Now the source is most of the visible sky, and there is not one cast shadow in the frame: nothing from the telephone pole onto the white clapboard behind it, nothing from the cars onto the road, only a faint darkening under the eaves. Nothing about the buildings changed. The source got bigger.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Hard and soft light — Image Wiki
answer:
Vilhelm Hammershøi, Interior, Sunlight on the Floor, 1906 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
Two sources of very different apparent size, in one room, and you can sort them out by looking at edges. The patch on the floor has crisp boundaries that reproduce the glazing bars of the window: that is direct sun, half a degree wide, projecting the shape of the opening it came through.
Everything else in the picture is lit by the sky through the same window — a source several feet across as the room sees it — and every one of its transitions is a gradual roll: down the panelled wall, around the door frame, across the tablecloth at the left. No traceable edge anywhere on them.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Hard and soft light — Image Wiki
answer:
Hard: Caravaggio, The Calling of Saint Matthew, 1599–1600
Soft: Vermeer, The Milkmaid, c. 1658


Two paintings, one variable. Both are lit from a high window on the right-ish side; the difference is the size of that window as the figures see it. Both images are in the public domain.
Caravaggio used a small, distant source. Watch the shadow the raised hand throws on the back wall — it has a definite edge, and you could trace it. Faces flip from lit to dark across a couple of centimetres of cheek.
Vermeer used a large one, close by. There is no traceable edge anywhere on the maid: her forehead darkens into her temple over the width of a thumb, and the wall behind her carries a shadow so gradual you have to hunt for where it starts. Same geometry, same sun, different apparent size.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Linear perspective — Image Wiki
answer:
Jack Delano, tracks at the Proviso yard of the Chicago and North Western Railroad, April 1943. FSA/OWI Kodachrome, Library of Congress. Public domain, US government work.
Put a fingertip where the rails appear to meet, near the middle of the frame: that is the vanishing point. Every rail in the yard arrives there, and so do the ballast edges and the yellow-painted rails down the centre — all of them parallel to one another on the ground, and one direction gets one point.
Then read the sleepers, identical planks at identical spacing. At the bottom of the frame each is a broad board with a gap you could put a boot into; a third of the way up they are a fine stripe; near the point they merge into grey.
Last, the two rows of boxcars: same-sized cars whose rooflines drop and wheels climb as they recede, pinching toward the height the rails converge on. That height is eye level, and it sits below the roof of the nearest car — Delano was on the ballast, not on a bridge.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Linear perspective — Image Wiki
answer:
The Ideal City, Urbino, c. 1480–1490, public domain.
The same geometry constructed rather than photographed: the rooflines, base lines, paving joints and door steps all run back to the doorway at the centre of the round building.
Look instead at what does not converge. The horizontal courses of stone across the building fronts run flat across the panel, and the columns and jambs stay upright. Those edges are parallel to the picture surface, so they never shrink toward anything — which is what makes this one-point, and tells you the painter stood square-on to the square.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Lines and movement — Image Wiki
answer:
Horizontals: Vernet, A Calm at a Mediterranean Port, 1770
Diagonals: Vernet, Storm with a Shipwreck, 1754


Claude-Joseph Vernet, A Calm at a Mediterranean Port, 1770, and Storm with a Shipwreck, 1754. Both public domain. Getty uses this same pair to teach horizontal and diagonal line.
One painter, one subject — a coast with a ship and some figures — and opposite dominant directions.
In the calm, list the horizontals: the sea's flat edge, the top of the harbour wall, the quay's coping, the stacked lengths of timber in the foreground, the reflected sun lying flat on the water. The only strong verticals are the lighthouse and the ship's masts, and both stand square. Nothing in the geometry is going anywhere.
In the storm, almost nothing is level. The wrecked ship's masts and yards make a bundle of crossing diagonals, the wave crests run up to the left, the shafts of rain slant, the great rock is a wedge, the men hauling on the rope lean into a diagonal of their own. The one thing standing upright is the tower on the right, and it reads as the only safe object in the picture.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Lines and movement — Image Wiki
answer:
Alfred Stieglitz, The Steerage, 1907 (Google Art Project). Public domain.
One line doing both jobs at once. The pale gangway runs from the lower left up to the right — the lightest, straightest, longest shape in the picture, and a diagonal.
As a divider it is absolute. The people above it and the people below it never mix; the frame is two populations, and that division is what the photograph is about.
As a link it is also the route across. Your eye gets from the lower deck to the upper one by running up it, and it makes the trip in one movement. Notice the bracing around it: the funnel at the left is a hard vertical, the ladder at the right a counter-diagonal offering a second and much slower way between the levels, and the sagging chains of the railing repeat the gangway's angle in miniature.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Lines and movement — Image Wiki
answer:
Albrecht Dürer, The Four Horsemen, from The Apocalypse, 1498, woodcut (National Gallery of Art, CC0).
Every mark here is a line, which makes it the clearest possible demonstration. Smarthistory's observation about the hat on one of the horsemen is worth stopping on: it is made of a few black contour strokes, and there is no hat there at all — only marks on paper that your eye agrees to treat as one (SRC-007).
Now count the directions. All four horses face right and the group drives left to right; their forelegs, the riders' bodies, the raised sword, the bow, the flying reins and the scales all repeat a bank of roughly parallel diagonals. The background is ruled with plain horizontal lines that shade the sheet and, at the same time, read as the ground streaming past.
The exception proves the rule. At the lower left the pit of hell and the bishop being swallowed are drawn in dense curls going nowhere, and that corner is the only part of the picture that feels stationary — because it is the only part with no diagonal in it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Lines and movement — Image Wiki
answer:
Leonardo da Vinci, The Virgin of the Rocks, c. 1483–86 (Musée du Louvre). Public domain.
Follow the eyes and the hands, in order. The angel on the right looks out of the picture at you, and points across it to the infant John on the left. John kneels with his hands together toward the infant Christ. Christ raises a hand back at him. Mary looks down at Christ, her right hand on John's shoulder and her left hovering above her son's head.
That is a closed circuit made of nothing. Smarthistory calls these sight lines and describes the effect precisely: you enter through the angel's gaze and are then locked into a cycle of movement between the figures (SRC-007). Not one of those lines exists as a mark on the panel, and they are the strongest structure in it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Logo reproduction tests — Image Wiki
answer:
NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.6 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
Nine numbered failures, and the giveaway is that they are numbered. This is not a designer's wish list; it is a list of things that had already been done to the mark. Note what kinds of things they are. 1, 7, 8: the solid stroke broken up by a pattern or a halftone screen, so the letters stop being one shape. 2, 3: the mark dropped inside a circle or a box, which is what happens when somebody needs it to fill a square slot. 4, 5: outlined and shadowed, the two standard ways of adding "impact" that dissolve the silhouette. 6: photographically distorted, here skewed into a fake italic. 9: turned on its side to fit a narrow gap.
Every one of these is a person solving a layout problem at 5pm. That is what the tests are defending against.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Logo reproduction tests — Image Wiki
answer:
NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.4 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
Three permitted versions on white, then the reversed one. The rules on this page are all about value, not taste: on black or very dark grounds the logotype is always white; on a medium-value ground it may be black or white, whichever reads; and NASA red is forbidden on medium, dark or black grounds — a saturated red against a dark ground has almost no lightness difference to work with, so the letters stop separating.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Map furniture and map colour — Image Wiki
answer:
The left half of the bottom margin, Ordnance Survey One-Inch Sheet 90, Wensleydale, published 1961. Crown copyright expired; public domain. Click to enlarge.
All administration, all of it kept off the map. REVISION INFORMATION — fully revised 1959, major roads revised 1966 — is the most useful line on the sheet, because it tells you which parts are eight years stale. The PUBLIC RIGHTS OF WAY box admits how far the footpath survey actually got; the yellow box gives the National Park designation and its 1954 confirmation order; the index to adjoining sheets boxes 90 among its neighbours so you know which map to buy next.
There is no ornamental north arrow. Instead two small star diagrams of magnetic, grid and true north, a table of the grid-north difference measured at each corner of this sheet (0°23′E at the north-west corner, 0°07′W at the south-east), and a note that magnetic north was about 9°W in 1967, decreasing by about half a degree every six years. That is the only orientation fact a compass user can act on, and it sits in the margin where nobody trips over it.
The scale bars run in both directions from zero, subdivided finely to the left of it and coarsely to the right, so you can measure a short distance and a long one with the same edge of paper.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Map furniture and map colour — Image Wiki
answer:
Willem Blaeu, Gviana sive Amazonvm Regio, Amsterdam, 1635. Public domain.
Every piece of furniture is here and every piece is decorated. The title sits in a carved cartouche; the scale bar has its own frame and gives two units, German and Gallic miles; the imprint sits in a third. Orientation is a compass rose with rhumb lines fanning across the whole sheet, plus SEPTENTRIO and MERIDIES lettered on the neat line — north and south spelled out because the arrow convention had not settled.
Then look at the middle: Parime Lacus, a large inland lake, drawn as confidently as the coast. It does not exist. Good furniture is not evidence.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: What a map decides — Image Wiki
answer:
Ordnance Survey One-Inch Sheet 90, Wensleydale, published 1961. Crown copyright expired; public domain. Click to enlarge.
A reference map with no single subject, so the hierarchy has to be subtle enough that a reader can pick their own. Six layers, from the back forward: a pale buff ground tint carrying thin orange contours; blue water; green woodland; the road network in red and yellow; black for buildings, tracks and symbols; and black type above everything.
The contours are the tell. They cover every square inch, they are the densest feature on the sheet, and they still lose — because they are drawn thin and pale, so the roads cross them without a fight. Squint and the red road along Wensleydale is the first thing you see. Nothing was deleted to achieve that.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: What a map decides — Image Wiki
answer:
John Snow, map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak; lithograph by C. F. Cheffins, London. Public domain. Commons dates this file to 1854; the sheet is headed Map 1, as it appeared in the 1855 second edition.
One question: where were the deaths, relative to the pumps? Everything on the sheet serves it and nothing else does. Deaths are stacked black bars at their addresses, so a bad house reads as a thick block. Pumps are dots labelled PUMP in the only bold word on the map. Buildings are hairline outlines with no fill, no relief, no land use, no tint.
Look at Broad Street, centre: a wall of black. Now look at the workhouse to the north-west and Golden Square to the south — big, populous, and almost blank. That contrast is the argument, and it is visible in about a second because Snow threw everything else away.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: What a map decides — Image Wiki
answer:
Admiralty Chart No. 2491, New York Harbour, United Kingdom Hydrographic Office, published 1857, corrected to 1867. Public domain.
Figure-ground, inverted on purpose. The water is the figure — thousands of engraved soundings, shoals, channels, the Sandy Hook bar. Manhattan and Brooklyn are the ground: a faint scribble of streets, unlabelled, with Long Island trailing off as a ghost. A city of several hundred thousand people has been reduced to the shape of an obstacle.
Note the extras that follow from the question. A table of lights top left. Coastal profile views along the bottom margin, drawn as the land looks from the sea at a stated bearing, because that is how you find the entrance. Useless for finding a hotel. Correct for not sinking.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: What a map decides — Image Wiki
answer:
What rock is under here: Smith, 1815
How do I get there: Cary, 1794


Left: William Smith, A Delineation of the Strata of England and Wales, with part of Scotland, 1815. Right: John Cary, Cary's New Map of England and Wales, with part of Scotland, 1794 (composite of the sheets). Both public domain.
The same island at almost the same date, drawn against different questions, and you can see which is which from across the room. On Smith's map the figure is colour: bands of strata sweeping south-east, with towns and roads ghosted underneath as thin grey. On Cary's, colour barely appears and the figure is the black mesh of post roads and place names; there is no geology at all, because a coach driver does not care.
Neither map answers the other's question. That is not a limitation of 18th-century printing — it is the choice being made properly.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Measure and line height — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "Understanding measure/line length". Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
One variable: the width of the block. Same typeface, same size, same leading. The first is short enough for a caption but chops prose into fragments; the second is still too short for paragraph text; the third is about right; the fourth is the one that makes you lose your place.
Look at what breaks in the fourth. It is not that the words are harder to read. It is that when you finish a line, the beginning of the next one is a long way back and slightly down, and there is nothing to aim at.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Measure and line height — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "Choosing a suitable line height" — too tight, just right, too open. Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
The pale blue bands are the baseline grid, so you can measure the change. Left, the descenders of one line reach the ascenders of the next and the block reads as a single grey mass. Right has the opposite failure: the lines are so far apart they stop belonging to the same paragraph, and your eye has to search downwards.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Measure and line height — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "Choosing a suitable line height". Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
The same passage at the same font size, twice. The narrow block gets tighter leading; the wide block gets more. Count the baseline-grid marks at the right-hand edge of each line to see the difference — this is the diagonal from the previous diagram, in real type.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Metal and everything else — Image Wiki
answer:
Conductor: a polished steel sphere outdoors
Dielectric: a glass ball held against the sky


Both figures by Scratchapixel, Reflection, Refraction and Fresnel, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source. Two spheres, the same problem, opposite answers — the band widths in the diagram above, photographed.
The steel sphere turns nearly everything back at its front face, so the front face is the whole picture: white sky along the top, a brick office block with pale columns and near-black windows across the middle, a dome at the right, paving slabs sweeping over the bottom, and the photographer standing in the middle of it. Follow the joints between the paving slabs — straight lines on the ground, bent into arcs on the ball. Nothing in it is steel-coloured: the brick comes back brick-red and the sky white.
The glass ball does the opposite with the same arriving light. A few per cent bounces off the boundary — the single sun glint near the top is most of it — and the rest goes in. What fills the ball is therefore the far side of the world, upside down: treetops hanging from the upper edge, the horizon line running across it, and the photographer's own fingertips showing through at the bottom.
Glass is the transparent extreme of the dielectric side, so nothing scatters inside it and it has no body colour of its own — that part it does not share with the porcelain and moss further down this page, whose pigment scatters what enters. The split at the boundary is the same either way: a few per cent off, the rest in.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Metal and everything else — Image Wiki
answer:
Mary Harrsch, Silver water jug by Obadiah Rich, Boston, 1845–1850, at the Portland Art Museum, 2012. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
Read the room off the jug. The olive-yellow gallery wall comes back as a warm band wrapped round the belly and neck; the dark band under it is the wood panelling; the pale wedge lower down is the plinth, and the fan-shaped streaks up on the shoulder are something overhead. Every value on this object is a value from somewhere else in the room.
Then notice what is not there: no silver-coloured shading, no lit side rolling smoothly into a dark side the way a ceramic jug would. Values jump from near-white to near-black within a centimetre, because neighbouring patches point at different things. And nothing is tinted — silver hands back the room's own colours, so the olive wall stays olive and the floor stays brown.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Metal and everything else — Image Wiki
answer:
Metal: a silver teapot, c. 1795
Non-metal: a porcelain teapot, 1662–1722


Two teapots photographed by the same museum against the same plain grey backdrop under the same soft light. The only variable that matters is which of the two laws the surface obeys.
The silver pot has no colour. Its flat oval body is a broad pale sweep of the backdrop, mottled but featureless — nothing in that room to be a picture of. The curved parts give it away: the lid squeezes the whole studio into two centimetres, near-white on top then a hard dark line where the light stops, and the spout carries a razor-thin dark stripe along its ridge with a bright one below.
The porcelain pot keeps its own colours — white ground, iron-red flowers, green leaves — and holds their value round the form, brightening only where it turns toward the light. Its specular contribution is the small white glints on the shoulder and lid. Those are the light; the flowers are the pot.
Left: John A. Schanck, teapot, c. 1795. Right: Chinese, small covered wine pot or teapot, 1662–1722. Both Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Metal and everything else — Image Wiki
answer:
R. Henrik Nilsson, Skultuna copper kettle, Skultuna, Sweden, presumably 1800s, 2024. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
The kettle does everything the silver jug did, with one addition. Follow the broad soft band down the right of the body: that is the bright sky, and it comes back copper-coloured, not white. The darker sweep across the left and lower body is the shaded ground, also coppery. Even at the base rim, where the surface points at the moss, the reflection turns a coppery green.
Compare the moss itself: green body colour held everywhere, a dull broad sheen instead of a mirror. A dielectric, and no amount of sunlight will make it show you the sky.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Motion as information — Image Wiki
answer:
Eadweard Muybridge, The Horse in Motion ("Sallie Gardner", Palo Alto track, 19 June 1878). Library of Congress; public domain.
Read the printed note under the plate: the negatives were made "at intervals of twenty-seven inches of distance, and about the twenty-fifth part of a second of time". Twelve frames, forty milliseconds apart, of one stride.
This is what a motion specification looks like — then and now. Nobody can argue about a movement while watching it at speed, so you stop it, lay the instants side by side, and check them one at a time. The vertical lines are 27 inches apart and the horizontals four inches, so you can measure the horse rather than admire it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Motion as information — Image Wiki
answer:
Étienne-Jules Marey, Chronophotograph of a Man on a Bicycle, c. 1885–1890. National Gallery of Art; CC0.
One plate, one rider, five exposures, and you read it instantly as a single man moving right — not as five men. That is continuity doing its work in a still image: same white jacket, same cap, same wheel, in a row.
The spacing is the other half. The gaps between the figures are near enough equal, which tells you the speed was steady. Later in this section that spacing becomes the diagnostic: unequal gaps mean acceleration, and acceleration is what an easing curve is.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Timing and restraint — Image Wiki
answer:
Étienne-Jules Marey, Chronophotograph of a Flying Heron, Cleveland Museum of Art. CC0.
An easing curve, photographed. The shutter opened at a fixed rate, so every gap between two birds is the same slice of time — which means the gaps are speed.
Start at the left, where the exposures pile on top of each other and the wings overlap: the heron is barely moving. Follow it right and the figures separate, then separate further, and the last two are further apart than any pair before them while also climbing. Crowded means slow, spread means fast. That is the whole grammar, and the plots below use it too.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Timing and restraint — Image Wiki
answer:
Phenakistiscope disc with cats and donkey, c. 1830. Cooper Hewitt collection; public domain.
Spun in front of a mirror and watched through the twelve slots, this disc plays about a second of animation: the cat clears the stool, the donkey chews. Then it plays it again. And again, identically, for as long as you keep spinning.
Every animation in an interface is one of these discs. The question is never how the movement feels once. It is how it feels on the fortieth spin.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Negative space — Image Wiki
answer:
Rubin's vase, after Edgar Rubin's 1915 figure. Drawing by Ian Remsen via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.
There is exactly one boundary in this picture and it does two jobs. Read the black as figure and you get two faces nose to nose. Read the white as figure and you get a stemmed vase. The pixels never change.
What you cannot do is hold both readings at once — try, and it flips. Neither reading is wrong; your visual system simply refuses to assign one contour to two objects simultaneously, and it will not let you opt out of choosing.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Negative space — Image Wiki
answer:
Caspar David Friedrich, The Monk by the Sea, 1808–10 (Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin). Public domain.
Three horizontal bands and one vertical mark. The sky takes roughly the top three quarters of the canvas, the sea is a narrow dark strip, and the pale shore fills the bottom. The only interruption anywhere is the monk — a dark upright taking up under a tenth of the picture's height, on a canvas 1.7 metres across.
Measure how little he is given and how much he gets: no detail, no face, no colour, no light on him. What makes him the subject is that he is the single event in an otherwise unbroken field, and that the two largest shapes in the picture have no other business.
This is also the cleanest test of the "empty space is wasted space" instinct. Crop to the monk and the shore and you still have a competent small picture of a figure on a beach. You have thrown away the entire meaning.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Negative space — Image Wiki
answer:
Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, c. 1831. The famous part is the wave. The reason it works is everything that is not the wave.
Look at the hollow between the crest and the boats — a large, clean, almost featureless shape. It is doing as much work as the wave: it is the only quiet area in the picture, so the eye rests there, and resting there is what makes you notice Mount Fuji sitting small in the gap. Fuji gets no detail and no contrast. It gets space, and space is enough.
Then cover the pale sky in the upper right with your thumb. The crest stops being enormous. It had nothing left to be big against. Public domain.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Packaging you can actually open — Image Wiki
answer:
Microsoft Packaging & Content Design, Creating Accessible Packaging: An Inclusive Design Toolkit, Spring 2026, page 30. © Microsoft, CC BY-NC-ND. Reproduced whole and unmodified.
Zoom in on the middle column, because it is the part designers never see written down. Opening must not need a force of operation over 3 lb (1.36 kg). The pack must open with one hand, and without the ability to pinch, to twist the wrist, or to grasp with the hand — three separate abilities, tested separately. Boxes over 5 lb must allow two hands. A graspable area must be no wider than 3 inches. No tools. If opening takes several actions, they must be performable one at a time.
Then read the two rules that sit in the left column as if they were graphics rules, because they are: text and graphics at a contrast ratio of at least 3:1, and colour never the only carrier of meaning.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Packaging you can actually open — Image Wiki
answer:
Microsoft Packaging & Content Design, Creating Accessible Packaging: An Inclusive Design Toolkit, Spring 2026, page 16. © Microsoft, CC BY-NC-ND. Reproduced whole and unmodified.
A pull tab drawn as an engineering part: units mm, scale 100%, six variants from 16.5 × 18 mm up to 36 × 30 mm, each with its corner radius called out (r7.5, r9, r18). The dark slot in the middle of every tab is a tactile element, not decoration.
The four guidance notes are the mechanism. Size the tab based on the effort needed to lift — force determines size, not the layout. Leave space around the tab for access, because a tab flush against a wall cannot be pinched. Adjust radius for strength, because a tight corner is where the card tears. And concentric alignment of tabs with wayfinding iconography — the printed arrow and the physical tab must share a centre, or the finger goes to the wrong place.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Packaging you can actually open — Image Wiki
answer:
Sokolikmawwer0, EAN-13 barcode on a gummy candy package, 2026. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
What a graded symbol looks like from a millimetre away. The bars are dark navy, not black, which GS1 permits, and the light background reads as the plain film rather than a printed white panel.
Now look at the bar edges. They are soft and slightly wavy, and the wide bars have spread into the spaces — ink gain, the normal behaviour of ink on flexible film. Edge sharpness and bar width are exactly what a verifier measures, which is why printers specify a bar width reduction in the artwork, shaving the bars so the printed result lands on target. The human-readable line carries all 13 digits, as EAN-13 requires; if the bars degrade past grading, that line is the fallback at the till.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Packaging hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
Wolfmann, SPAR Tjøme, Norway, breakfast cereal shelves, 31 August 2023. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
Look at the AXA range in the second row and count what is identical: the red wordmark, the white oval it sits in, the position of that oval, the photograph of the contents filling the lower half, and a percentage in a circle. Only two things change between flavours — one word set in heavy capitals (BLÅBÆR, HASSELNØTT) and the colour of the band behind it (navy, plum, brown).
That is the hierarchy working: the constant part does the shelf-identification job at a metre, the two changing parts do the variant job, and the six-point strapline under the oval ("MED HAVRE OG SPRØ FLAKES") is only readable in the hand — which is where it belongs. Note also what is not on the pack: the price is on the shelf rail.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Packaging hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
Clifford H. Poland, Interior view of a Piggly Wiggly self-service grocery store, 1918. Library of Congress, public domain. The credit line "©1918 Clarence Saunders" is printed on the original photograph.
The moment the problem was invented. Shelves are open, the counter clerk is gone, and for the first time a shopper is alone with the packages. Now look at what the packages are doing about it: nothing. Every can carries a small paper label with a wreath and a paragraph of roman type, all at the same weight, so from where the camera stands you cannot tell one from another — the shopkeeper's numbered signs hanging from the shelf edge ("SECTION 2") are doing the identification work instead.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Packaging hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
2006 label: Calories set small, beside Calories from Fat
2016 label: Calories in large bold type, Added Sugars added


FDA's own illustrations of the label before and after the 2016 update. Both public domain (US federal work). Read the layout, not the numbers: the sugars figures differ between the two examples.
Left, everything competes. "Calories 230" is set at the same size as "Total Fat", with "Calories from Fat 40" sitting next to it at equal weight, and a second table of 2,000/2,500-calorie reference values fills the bottom third.
Right, one number wins. "Calories" is large and bold, "230" is larger still and pushed to the right margin; "servings per container" moves above "Serving size", which is now bold on its own line. "Calories from Fat" is gone. "Includes 10g Added Sugars" is indented under "Total Sugars". Vitamins A and C are out; vitamin D and potassium are in, each with an actual amount beside its percentage. The reference table is replaced by one sentence of footnote.
The percentages moved too, on the same food: 8 g of total fat was 12% of a daily value in 2006 and is 10% now, because the Daily Values themselves were updated (PACK-008). A layout can be re-ranked without a single ingredient changing.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Testing whether a symbol works — Image Wiki
answer:
Photo: Cassian Lodge, department guide at Bronglais General Hospital, Aberystwyth, 2023, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0. Cropped to three of the four zone columns.
Look down the purple column: Rhiannon Short Stay Ward, Enlli and Ystwyth Wards, Leri Day Unit and Y Banwy all use the bed. In blue, so do Angharad Children's Ward, Meurig Ward and Dyfi. The symbols still work as a class marker — bed means inpatient — but they no longer separate one destination from another, so the reader is back to reading the text.
Two good decisions are visible too. The board is split into four colour zones, which is how you keep the number of symbols in view at any one time small. And the fork-and-knife for the dining room sits on a black disc rather than a coloured bar, marking it as a support destination rather than a department.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The first read — Image Wiki
answer:
Arthur Rothstein, See America — Welcome to Montana, United States Travel Bureau, made by the Works Progress Administration Federal Art Project, New York, between 1936 and 1938. Public domain (Library of Congress).
Squint at this, or scroll until it is thumbnail-sized, and count what is left: one big rust-brown mountain silhouette, a pale sky, a blue band of water, a pale teepee and a dark one at the bottom left, and two lines of type. Almost nothing in the picture is drawn — it is built from flat areas of six colours, and every boundary between two areas is also a value step, light against dark, so the shapes hold when the colour is stripped out. The only drawn marks in the whole sheet are the thin petroglyph figures on the pale teepee, and they are second-read material.
Then look at what the poster gave up to get that. There is no texture, no modelling, no detail small enough to reward standing close. The second read here is thin on purpose: this sheet was made to work on a wall you walk past.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The first read — Image Wiki
answer:
Survives the thumbnail: Flagg, 1917
Does not: Lumley, 1915


Two British and American army recruiting posters from the same war, with the same job, taking opposite bets. Both public domain.
Left (Flagg, 1917) is built for the first read. One head against an empty cream ground, the dark blue coat and hat band making a single mass, and four words in slab capitals across the bottom third at a size you can read from across a street. Cover the text and the pointing fist still says you. Cover the image and "I WANT YOU" still says it. Either half survives alone.
Right (Lumley, 1915) has almost no first read. The values are all mid-tones — brown jacket, green chair, blue carpet, tan wall — so at thumbnail size it collapses into an even mush with no shape to grab. The only text is a line of thin script at the very bottom, and it is the entire message. Cover it and the poster becomes a family photograph. This is a design that requires you to already be standing still.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The first read — Image Wiki
answer:
Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Moulin Rouge: La Goulue, 1891. Public domain.
An 1891 poster that passes the squint test better than most work made this year, and the reason is that it is built from three values and nothing else. Near-black: the band of top-hatted spectators across the middle and the row of dark legs. Near-white: the dancer's petticoat, the single brightest area in the sheet and therefore the first thing you see. Mid-grey: the enormous foreground figure of Valentin, deliberately flattened to a silhouette with no interior detail at all.
Follow the yellow lamp globes as a second layer, then the red letters. Nothing here is shaded, and no edge needs resolving — which is why the design still reads at the size of a postage stamp, and why the crowd behind can be a solid black shape without anyone feeling cheated.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Poster mechanisms — Image Wiki
answer:
Focus the eye: Flagg, 1917
Overwhelm the eye: Strobridge Litho. Co., 1899


Two mechanisms that Cooper Hewitt lists as neighbours and opposites. Both public domain.
Left, James Montgomery Flagg, I Want You for U.S. Army, 1917. One head, dead centre, filling two thirds of the sheet, with a pointing fist thrust forward at you and four words underneath. There is nothing else in the frame to look at. That is focus the eye.
Right, The Barnum & Bailey Greatest Show on Earth, printed by the Strobridge Lithographing Company, 1899. Count the things competing for you: twelve tents, thirty-odd flags, a locomotive, seven wagons, a crowd, two bands of shouting type. Your eye starts a tour and never settles. That is overwhelm the eye, and for a circus it is the honest answer — the promise is abundance, so the poster is made of abundance.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Poster mechanisms — Image Wiki
answer:
El Lissitzky, Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge, 1919. Public domain.
Four mechanisms in one sheet, and you can point at each. Activate the diagonal: the wedge runs corner to corner, so the eye crosses the whole surface instead of resting in the middle. Simplify: two shapes, three colours, no drawing. Manipulate scale: the wedge and circle are enormous, the scattered bars tiny, and that size gap alone reads as force meeting mass.
And use text as image — the words are not a caption sitting under a picture. Each phrase is placed inside the shape it describes, the red words on the red side, the white words inside the circle, so the sentence and the diagram are the same object. Note what is not here: no face, no story, no eye contact. Those mechanisms were available and were declined.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Poster mechanisms — Image Wiki
answer:
Savile Lumley, Daddy, what did YOU do in the Great War?, published by the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee, 1915. Public domain.
Tell a story, run all the way. Nothing in this poster is dramatic: a patterned curtain, a green armchair, a girl with a picture book on her father's knee, a small boy on the carpet lining up toy soldiers and a toy field gun. The work is done by a question in the title and a gaze — the father is the only figure who is not looking at the book, and he is not looking at you either. He stares past the edge of the frame with his knuckles at his mouth.
That combination sets a time bomb: the scene is the future, the question has already been asked, and you supply the answer. Compare it with the Flagg poster above. Same war, same purpose, opposite mechanism — and note the cost. This one has no first read at all. From across a street it is a brown domestic interior with a line of script along the bottom.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Print-ready files — Image Wiki
answer:
David Peters, Offset printing at Watermark Press, San Francisco — a press check for the Wiki Education Foundation's Editing Wikipedia guide on a Komori eight-colour perfector, 21 June 2016. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
What your file actually becomes. On the inspection table lies one press sheet holding many booklet pages at once, and look at their orientation: the whole upper row is upside down relative to the lower row, where the cover ("Editing Wikipedia") and the markup cheatsheet sit the right way up. That is imposition — the page order you designed has nothing to do with the arrangement that folds and binds correctly, and the printer decides it.
Then follow the very top edge of the sheet: a thin strip of repeating small patches of cyan, magenta, yellow, black and their overprints, running its whole length. That is the colour control bar, measured to check ink density across the sheet.
That strip lives outside the trimmed pages, in the area the guillotine removes. Marks, colour bars and bleed all share the same real estate: the part of the sheet nobody ever sees.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Rhythm and repetition — Image Wiki
answer:
Prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, begun 785. Photograph by James (Jim) Gordon via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Count the ways this picture repeats: one column type, one arch shape, one red-and-white voussoir stripe, one spacing, repeated in two directions until it runs out of building. Nothing here is the subject, and nothing needs to be — the repetition itself is what you are looking at, and it produces total unity out of several hundred separate stones.
Now find the people. There is a child in a pale top walking between columns in the left third, and two seated visitors by the far wall on the right, next to a thin vertical slit of daylight. Each of them is small, low-contrast and easy to miss in a verbal description — and each of them is the first thing your eye lands on once you know they exist. They are the only objects in the frame that are not members of the set.
This also shows the cost. Look for thirty seconds and the arches stop registering. There is no interval anywhere that differs from any other, so after the third bay there is nothing left to find out, and the eye disengages.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Rhythm and repetition — Image Wiki
answer:
Utagawa Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake, from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1857 (Library of Congress). Public domain.
Two rhythms doing opposite jobs in one print. The rain is one repeated mark — a long straight line — printed as two overlapping sets at slightly different angles, with uneven gaps. Nothing about it is measured, and that is why it reads as weather rather than as hatching: irregular intervals feel alive.
Under the bridge, the trestle is the other kind. Vertical posts at an even spacing, each with the same diagonal brace, repeated until the frame cuts it off — measured, still, structural.
Then the five people. They are the exception in a frame where almost everything is a member of some set, and they are what you look at, even though they are small, dark and low in contrast against the pale deck. The lone raftsman out on the water gets the same treatment: he is the only mark in an empty band.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Rhythm and repetition — Image Wiki
answer:
The Pont du Gard, Roman aqueduct near Vers-Pont-du-Gard, first century CE. Photograph by Benh Lieu Song via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Three tiers, three cadences, one arch shape. The top arcade repeats at a spacing so short and so even that you give up counting arches after four or five and read the whole thing as a band — it has crossed over from being a row of objects into being a surface. That crossing is the subject of Shape, texture and pattern.
The tall middle arcade does the opposite. Its arches are large and deliberately unequal: the widest one straddles the river channel, and they narrow as they go left across the gorge. So the point where the bridge crosses the water is marked by an interval rather than by an ornament — nothing was added there, one gap is simply bigger.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The rule of thirds — Image Wiki
answer:
Centred, deliberately: Raphael, La Donna Velata, c. 1512–15
Off centre, deliberately: Winslow Homer, Breezing Up, 1873–76


Raphael, La Donna Velata, c. 1512–15 (Palazzo Pitti, Florence). Winslow Homer, Breezing Up (A Fair Wind), 1873–76 (National Gallery of Art, Washington). Both public domain.
Raphael puts the head within a hair of the vertical axis and gives it a plain dark ground. Nothing in the picture happens off to one side, so nothing pulls your eye off the face; she looks back out at you and the exchange is head-on. Slide her onto a third and you would be watching her instead of meeting her.
Homer does the opposite, and you can check it with a ruler. The boat and its sail fill the left two thirds; the right third is open water and sky, with one small distant schooner in it to prove the space is deep. The horizon runs low, so the sky takes the larger share of the height too. What the off-centre placement buys is somewhere for the eye to go after the boat: slide the boat to the middle and you get two matched gaps, neither worth crossing.
Neither placement is a compliance result. Each follows from one question: is this subject looking at the viewer, or is it doing something inside the frame?

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The rule of thirds — Image Wiki
answer:
Jacob van Ruisdael, View of Haarlem with Bleaching Grounds, c. 1670–75 (Mauritshuis, The Hague). Public domain.
Find the horizon: the city silhouette runs across at roughly two thirds of the way down, and the church of St Bavo stands a little left of centre. Painted two centuries before anyone drew a thirds grid on a viewfinder.
The reason the fraction matters is visible if you imagine it moved. As it stands the sky has more room than the land, so the weather is the event and Haarlem is a detail underneath it — which is what the picture is about. Drop the horizon to the middle and you get two roughly equal bands, sky and land, with no answer to which one you are looking at.
Note also what the low horizon buys in the foreground: the sunlit strips of bleaching linen read as a clear shape because there is enough land to hold them. Composition here is a division of area, not a placement of dots.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The rule of thirds — Image Wiki
answer:
Giovanni Paolo Panini, Interior of the Pantheon, Rome, c. 1734 (National Gallery of Art, Washington). CC0.
The formal case, two centuries before Kubrick. Panini stands almost on the building's axis: the tall doorway in the far wall and the arch above it sit within a few per cent of the vertical centre line, and the dome's rings come round symmetrically on both sides of it. The floor's paving runs straight at you.
Move any of that onto a third and the subject — a perfectly circular room that is the same in every direction — stops being describable. The oculus is the one thing off centre, a little to the right, and the patch of sun it throws high on the left-hand coffers is what keeps the picture from going inert. The figures are scattered asymmetrically for the same reason: symmetry for the architecture, and life allowed to be untidy inside it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The rule of thirds — Image Wiki
answer:
Ansel Adams, The Tetons and the Snake River, Grand Teton National Park, 1942. National Archives; taken for the Department of the Interior, public domain.
Watch your own eye instead of the grid. It goes first to the brightest thing in the frame — the lit S-curve of the river — then follows that curve back and up into the dark bank of trees, then jumps to the sunlit snow on the peaks, and only afterwards notices the lit cloud in the top left. Hierarchy did all of that, by value.
Now try to score the picture on thirds. The tallest peak sits a little right of the middle. The horizon is about halfway up. The river crosses everywhere and lands on nothing. A grid checker would mark this down, and it is one of the most looked-at landscape photographs ever made.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Scale and proportion — Image Wiki
answer:
No reference object: the pillars could be two metres or twenty
One human figure on the ridge, and the pillars are settled


Rock pillars (kigilyakh) of the Ulakhan-Sis range, Sakha, northern Siberia. Photograph by Artem Abdukakharov via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. The left panel is our own crop of the same photograph, taken from the left of the frame; nothing else was changed.
Left. Try to say how tall these are. You cannot, and the frustrating part is that nothing is missing — the rock is sharp, well lit, and clearly described. The lichen and the loose blocks in the foreground hint at a metre or so, so most people guess low: garden boulders, a stone circle, a few metres at most.
Right. One person, standing on the ridge to the right, and the guess collapses into a fact. The pillars are roughly ten times a person, so somewhere in the region of fifteen metres — five storeys of rock. Nothing about the stone changed between the two panels. Your knowledge of how tall people are did the entire job.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Scale and proportion — Image Wiki
answer:
Albert Bierstadt, The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak, 1863 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
All four cues at once, on purpose. The bottom fifth of the canvas is an encampment: tipis, horses, dogs, dozens of people. Measure one standing figure against the waterfall behind it, then against the snowfield above that, and the mountain sizes itself.
The long distances are carried by the other three. The peaks are pale, blue and almost without detail, while the foreground grass has individual blades; the trees on the middle ridges are separate crowns at the near edge and an even nap at the far one.
Cover the encampment with your hand. The picture still reads as mountains — but as mountains of no particular size, and most of its drama leaves with the horses.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Scale and proportion — Image Wiki
answer:
Leonardo da Vinci, Vitruvian Man, c. 1490 (Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice). Public domain.
A drawing about proportion and nothing else, and there is no reference object anywhere in it — which is the point. Everything here is a comparison of one part of the body with another part.
Look at the two enclosing figures. The square works because the arm span equals the standing height; put your fingers on the fingertips and the toes and you can check it. The circle is centred not on the chest but on the navel, and it is the arms-raised, legs-apart pose that touches it. Two different claims about the same body, drawn on top of each other.
Then look for the measuring apparatus. There is a graduated bar under the feet, and short tick marks across the forearms and along the raised arms. Leonardo is dividing the figure into named fractions, exactly as Vitruvius specified them — and the fractions are plain ones: a tenth, an eighth, a sixth. No irrational numbers were required.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The anatomy of a shadow — Image Wiki
answer:
Francisco de Zurbarán, Still Life with Lemons, Oranges and a Rose, 1633 (Norton Simon Museum, Pasadena). Public domain.
Every zone in the list, on real objects, under one source. The light comes from the upper left: all three cast shadows — of the plate of lemons, of the basket, of the cup — run to the right, and each object's lit face is its upper left.
Take the lemon on the left of the pewter plate. Its highlight is a soft pale patch on the upper left of the skin, broad rather than a dot, because a lemon is matte. The halftone covers most of the rest of the peel, changing so gradually you cannot say where it begins. The core shadow is the darkest part of the fruit itself, along its lower right — and it stops short of the silhouette, because a thin strip of reflected light off the plate lifts the bottom of the lemon back out of the dark. Compare that strip against the lit top of the same lemon: unmistakably darker. That is the rule that keeps the fruit reading as solid.
Then the two shadows on the table. The cast shadow to the right of the plate is a soft, open grey — blocked from the window but still lit by the rest of the room. The contact shadow under the rim of the plate is a near-black hairline, because nothing gets into that seam at all. Cover the fruit and the plate still reads as sitting on the wood, from that line alone.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The anatomy of a shadow — Image Wiki
answer:
Juan Sánchez Cotán, Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber, c. 1602 (San Diego Museum of Art). Public domain.
The same painting runs the experiment twice, and the difference is whether there is anything nearby to catch light or throw it back. One small hard source enters from the upper left: the cut wedge and the cucumber each lay a crisp-edged shadow to the right along the stone ledge, and each has a dark seam where it touches.
On the ledge, the objects get the full sequence — cast shadow, contact seam, and a shadow side kept well above black by the pale stone underneath. Hanging in the void, the quince and the cabbage get none of it: no floor, no wall, nothing behind them, so their shaded sides fall away toward the black of the ground and neither casts a shadow anywhere in the picture. Same painter, same light, same day. Both cast shadows and reflected light need a second surface to exist at all.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Shape, texture and pattern — Image Wiki
answer:
Katsushika Hokusai, Fine Wind, Clear Morning (Gaifū kaisei), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, c. 1830–32 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
All three, in one print, kept separate on purpose.
Shape. Fuji is a single flat area of pink-brown with an outline and nothing inside it but a few snow streaks. No modelling, no gradient, no attempt at a volume — and it is instantly a mountain.
Texture. The forest along the lower slope is thousands of small dark marks. Follow it from right to left: near the right they are separated enough that you can pick out an individual tree, and by the left they have merged into an even dark nap where no single mark is findable. That is the shape-to-texture crossing happening inside one band of one picture.
Pattern. The sky is a repeated cloud bar, stacked at regular intervals. You read it once, predict the rest, and stop looking — which is exactly what it is for. The clouds are numerous and high in contrast, and they still do not compete with the mountain.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Shape, texture and pattern — Image Wiki
answer:
The Palouse hills from Steptoe Butte, Whitman County, Washington. Photograph by Caleb Riston via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
The sun is low and almost sideways, so every hill casts a shadow onto the next one. What you are looking at is not a pattern of dark paint on the ground; it is a field of cast shadows, and it is the reason this landscape has a surface at all.
Then walk your eye from the bottom of the frame to the top. In the foreground each hill is a shape with its own lit face and its own shadow, big enough to hold a farm. Halfway up, the hills are still separable but you have stopped counting them. At the horizon they have become an even fine texture in which no individual hill exists.
One photograph, one hillside type, one light. The rung you are on is decided entirely by how much of the frame each hill occupies.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Shape, texture and pattern — Image Wiki
answer:
Tilework of the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, Isfahan, completed 1619. Photograph by Swissfrog via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
Two patterns, doing opposite jobs, in one frame.
The dome at the lower right is a grid of identical lozenges that shrinks steadily towards the crown. It is completely predictable, so within a second you stop reading tiles and start reading a curved surface — the pattern's job here is to make you see a dome, and it does it by getting smaller.
The blue arabesque on the vaults above is much denser and far less predictable. Look closely and it is a repeated floral unit; look normally and it refuses to resolve, so it reads as a continuous field with no findable subject. It swallows anything placed on it, which is precisely why the band of white calligraphy running between the vaults sits on a plain dark ground instead. Change nothing about the writing and put it on the arabesque, and it disappears.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Shape, texture and pattern — Image Wiki
answer:
Attic black-figure neck-amphora, near the Medea Group, c. 510 BCE (J. Paul Getty Museum, CC0 via the Getty Open Content Program).
The same three rungs, this time on one pot, and useful because the shapes are literally flat.
Shape. Achilles and Ajax are solid black silhouettes. There is no shading and no volume, and you still read two armoured men leaning in over a board, plus Athena standing between them — because the outlines were designed to be legible. Notice what the painter did with the helmet crests and the spear shafts: they break the silhouette, so they read instantly.
Texture. Look inside the black. The scale armour, the shield rims and the hair are fine incised lines scratched through the slip. Individually they are invisible from a metre away; together they say metal, wool, hair.
Pattern. Three bands — palmettes at the neck, a meander below the figures, petals at the foot — each regular enough that you check a couple of units and accept the rest. They frame without competing, which is what patterns are for on an object whose subject is in the middle.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Sign legibility is arithmetic — Image Wiki
answer:
Photo: Eddau, 2007, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
A room sign built to the pattern: raised sans-serif capitals, Grade 2 braille directly under each line of characters, and the pictogram field kept clear of both. The raised characters must be uppercase — a rule about fingertips rather than eyes, since a tactile reader tracks a constant-height band. Note also that the braille is not required to contrast with the plate, only the visual and raised characters are.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Sign legibility is arithmetic — Image Wiki
answer:
Photo: Hugh Llewelyn, Oval Underground Station (Northern Line), 2025, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
Two words, all capitals, white on dark blue vitreous enamel — and it works, because WAY OUT is a fixed phrase you recognise as a shape and never actually read. The arrow carries as much of the message as the words. Note the finish: enamel is glossy but the panel sits flat on a wall lit from the platform, and TfL's standards handle the remaining risk by controlling sightlines instead — exclusion zones around signs so departure indicators cannot block them, and repeater signs where the distance is too great.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Simplification — Image Wiki
answer:
Vilhelm Hammershøi, Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams, 1900 (Ordrupgaard, Copenhagen). Public domain.
Count what is in this painting. A window, a door, a skirting, a floor, and a wedge of light. No person, no furniture, no object, no incident, and almost no colour.
Now count the decisions. The window is placed off centre and pushed up so the floor gets the bottom third to itself. The wedge of sunlight enters from the right at an angle that crosses both the door and the floor, tying two flat planes together — take it away and the picture becomes two rectangles side by side. The panelled door is a fraction lighter than the wall it sits in, which is the only thing separating them.
That is why it is simple rather than empty: nothing here is available to remove. Delete any one of those five elements and something stops working.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Simplification — Image Wiki
answer:
Simplify: Toulouse-Lautrec, Divan Japonais, 1893
Overwhelm: Bruegel, The Fight Between Carnival and Lent, 1559


Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Divan Japonais, 1893. Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Fight Between Carnival and Lent, 1559 (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna). Both public domain.
Lautrec throws almost everything away. Jane Avril is one flat black shape from hat to hem — no folds, no modelling, no detail inside the silhouette — and the only marks allowed inside it are her face and two hands. Behind her the stage, the chairs and the orchestra are a grey wash with outlines. He even crops the singer at the top left so that her head is gone above the frame edge, leaving a body and two black gloves — a second face there would compete with the one he wants you to read.
Bruegel does the opposite deliberately. There are around two hundred figures, no focal point, and roughly even weight across the whole panel; the picture works as a field you graze rather than an arrangement you read. It has a structure — the two processions meeting in the middle — but that structure is a rule for the crowd, not a hierarchy that hands you a subject.
Neither is a botched version of the other. What would be botched is Bruegel's density with Lautrec's single subject buried inside it.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Simplification — Image Wiki
answer:
Detroit Publishing Co., Mulberry St., New York, N.Y., c. 1900 (Library of Congress). Public domain.
Hundreds of people, dozens of pushcarts, awnings, fire escapes, laundry, signage. By the arithmetic at the top of this article it should be unreadable, and it is not.
What holds it is structure rather than restraint. Two tenement walls converge on a bright gap of sky at the centre, so the frame has a route through it before you have identified a single person. The crowd sorts into three value bands — dark clothing at the bottom, pale awnings across the middle, dark buildings above. And the repeated units help: once you have read one pushcart you have read forty.
This is the honest limit of "remove things". You could not simplify this photograph without destroying its subject, which is the density itself.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Six frames from a free library, with what each one leaves out. Nothing here is badly made — the exposure is clean, the colour is neutral, somebody placed the light.
What they share is an absence: no city, no season, no company, no task you could name, and a patch of quiet wall where somebody else's headline will go.
Photographs by Kristin Hardwick, Helloquence, Christina Morillo (two frames) and Startup Stock Photos (two frames), from StockSnap, which releases everything on the site under CC0.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
The shapes that recur, and what each is a signal of. The handshake: an agreement with no parties, no place and no terms. The thumbs up: approval with nothing being approved. The lightbulb: the word "idea" photographed instead of an idea. The team with no roles: a room of people and not one job being done. Delight at a screen: the emotion has become the whole subject. The workspace: props arranged for a photograph rather than for work.
Photographs by Kristin Hardwick, Matt Moloney, Andrew E. Weber, Direct Media, Bruce Mars and Startup Stock Photos, from StockSnap, CC0.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: a warm two-colour bakery badge on cream, arched slab-serif name, a small line-drawn baker on a bike, FRESH and BAKED in little pills
Generated: the marketplace badge template — a heavy double ring with the town arched above and the name arched below, a fully rendered cartoon cyclist with a basket of baguettes in the middle


The prompt: ""Bread Bike" badge logo, 'San Luis Obispo', character riding bicycle delivering bread".
The reference prints in one colour and survives being an inch wide. The generated mark is the marketplace template: double ring, town arched over the top, name arched under the bottom, and a fully drawn cyclist with individually modelled baguettes in the middle. It carries more ink, not less — measured detail is five times the reference's and contrast three times — and none of it identifies anybody.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: a thin white line-art ice-cream sandwich with a small face on a flat blue field, retro type with small arrows
Generated: a shaded cartoon sandwich with large googly eyes, blushed cheeks and two waving gloved hands, under outlined display type


The prompt: ""SAMMIES Ice Cream" logo, retro mascot style, ice cream sandwich character, blue and white".
One line-art mascot on a flat field becomes a shaded character with eyes, cheeks and waving hands — a figure sold by the thousand under "cute food mascot". Detail measures nearly five times the reference, and the retro restraint the prompt asked for is gone.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: a very small cow silhouette with a barn tucked into its body as negative space, delicate at that size
Generated: a large heavy cow silhouette with a crude gabled house punched out of its flank, filling the frame


The prompt: " logo mark, cow and house negative space silhouette".
Same idea in both: a barn inside a cow. The reference is tiny and reads as one mark. The generated one inflates it to fill the frame and punches out a plain gabled house, so the cut-out stops being a discovery and becomes the stock trick it is named after.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: a sitting cat drawn with thin legs, large round white eyes, fine whiskers and distinct paws and tail
Generated: a rounded chunky cat blob with small eyes, simplified paws and no whisker detail


The prompt: "mascote logo, Cute sitting black cat, minimal flat vector style, simple silhouette with whiskers, white background".
Nothing is added here and nothing is broken; the drawing simply loses its hand. Thin legs become a solid block, the round eyes shrink, the whiskers thin to nothing. Measured detail drops to seven tenths of the reference, which for a two-colour mark is most of what there was.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: hundreds of very fine concentric grooves in dark red terracotta, fine enough to interfere into a moiré
Generated: a coarse spiral of about thirty thick smooth ridges in flat orange, each with a soft plastic highlight


The prompt: "Close-up of concentric ripple grooves in red terracotta surface, fingerprint-like pattern filling entire frame, abstract texture".
The prompt asked for fingerprint-like ripple grooves. The reference has them by the hundred, fine enough that they interfere into a moiré at page size. The generated frame keeps the idea of concentric ripples and spends about thirty fat ridges on it, each with a soft highlight that reads as plastic. Measured detail: a third of the reference.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: a dense Liberty ditsy floral, pink, red, blue and yellow flowers with green leaves packed edge to edge on warm white
Generated: pale sparse sprigs on cream with large empty gaps between them


The prompt: "Liberty-style ditsy floral fabric pattern, cream background".
This is the one to remember for "washed out". Same brief, and the generated version drops to a third of the reference's detail, half its contrast and a third of its colour. The flowers get smaller, fewer and paler, and the cloth stops being a Liberty print and becomes generic wallpaper.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: a real ceramic elephant with a matte speckled glaze, titanium-oxide crust and uneven greens and greys over a visible clay body
Generated: a smooth chromed silver figurine with clean reflections on a grey ground


The prompt: "Primitive abstract ceramic elephant-like, colored glaze, titanium oxide, side, studio photo".
The prompt named the material — coloured glaze, titanium oxide, primitive ceramic. What comes back is chrome: one smooth reflective surface with no crust, no speckle and no clay. Detail measures four tenths of the reference and the colour is down to a third.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: The stock look — Image Wiki
answer:
Reference: an acid-yellow poster with distorted orange display type overlapping a small image box and a dense hand-set lineup in condensed caps
Generated: a tidy olive poster with clean red and black display type and a short centred lineup in even lines


The prompt: """AMSTERDAMSE BOS SUNDAY" electronic music festival poster, bold distorted typography, olive green background, red and dark grey lettering, artist lin".
The prompt asked for bold distorted typography. The generated poster is perfectly readable and perfectly ordinary: type set straight, lineup reduced to a few centred lines, ground shifted to a safe olive. Contrast and detail both land near half the reference's.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Type anatomy — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "An overview of Latin type anatomy" (typeface: Epilogue). Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
Follow the H: it starts at the cap-height line, not at the ascender line above it — in most faces the ascender of a lowercase l runs slightly taller than a capital. The p is the only letter here crossing the baseline, and its tail is what your line height has to leave room for.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Type anatomy — Image Wiki
answer:
Google Fonts Knowledge, "An overview of Latin type anatomy" (typeface: EB Garamond). Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
The ligature in the middle is the thing to look at: f and i have been replaced by a single drawn shape, so the f's hook does not crash into the i's dot. Two characters, one glyph. The small cap on the right is a third case form — an uppercase letter redrawn to sit at lowercase height, not a shrunken capital.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Type hierarchy on a page — Image Wiki
answer:
Playbill of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, Thursday 30 September 1784, announcing The Clandestine Marriage. Bodleian Libraries, John Johnson Collection of Printed Ephemera; public domain.
The opposite position, taken to its limit: this sheet has roughly a dozen sizes and almost no space. Every line is centred on one axis, every line is a different size, and hierarchy is done by magnitude alone. The two biggest lines are the two plays; the actors' surnames are pushed up in wide-spaced capitals while their roles stay small and lower case, so Lord Ogleby by Mr. is quiet and KING is loud, in the middle of the same line.
It is not incompetence — it works, and it worked for two centuries. But count the costs. There is no first read: nothing here survives being seen from three metres away. Nothing can be skimmed, because there are no groups, only a gradient. And every new line was a fresh decision for the compositor, which is exactly what a system is meant to eliminate.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Type hierarchy on a page — Image Wiki
answer:
Have a Date with Us, made by NYC WPA War Services for the American Museum of Natural History, 1941. Public domain (Library of Congress).
Count the type sizes and you get about eight, which by Vignelli's standard is a mess. It is not a mess, and the reason is that almost none of the levels are marked by size alone.
Colour does the top split: everything orange is the invitation, everything olive-brown is the detail, so "FREE TO YOU / AND YOUR FRIENDS" separates from the list below it before you have read a word. Position does the next one — the whole text block sits inside a ragged white patch painted over the picture, which is what keeps eight sizes of type from fighting the totem pole. Case does the finest one: in "AMERICAN MUSEUM of NATURAL HISTORY", every word is the same size, and the emphasis comes from alternating white against brown and dropping the connective to lower case. Two words are promoted and one demoted without touching a size.
The one thing size is used for here is the diagonal red line, which is the only element aimed at someone walking past. Everything else is second-read material, sorted by other means.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Type scales and spacing scales — Image Wiki
answer:
Named steps, 1734
Numbered steps, 1969


Left: William Caslon, A Specimen, London, 1734 (public domain). Right: a page of Granjon from Specimen of Type Faces in the United States Government Printing Office, 1969 — a US government work, so public domain.
Left is a type scale three hundred years before the phrase existed, and every step has a name: French Cannon, Two Lines Great Primer, Double Pica, Great Primer, English, Pica, Small Pica, Long Primer, Brevier, Nonpareil, Pearl. A printer did not ask for 15 point. He asked for Long Primer, because that was one of the sizes that existed in the shop.
Right, the same logic with numbers: Granjon at 12, 14, 21, 24 and 30 point, each with a case number — 43L12, 43L14, 43L21, 43L24, 43L30 — so a compositor could find the drawer. Now look at 21 point next to 24 point and try to tell them apart at a glance. You cannot, quickly, and that pair is exactly what a modern scale would drop.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Value structure — Image Wiki
answer:
Streeton's painting as he painted it
Lightness only — our own luminosity conversion
Hue and chroma only — our own, with lightness flattened


Arthur Streeton, Sunlight Sweet, Coogee, 1890. Public domain. The middle and right panels are ours: the middle keeps each pixel's lightness and throws the colour away, the right keeps hue and chroma exactly as painted and flattens lightness to one value.
The middle panel loses all the colour and loses nothing else. The white path, the dark cliff, the tree mass, the girl in the hat, the crowd on the skyline — every shape you needed is still there, and it would still read at thumbnail size.
The right panel is the one to sit with. Every colour is untouched, and the picture is gone: a soft smear in which the only findable things are the red figure and a few blue-grey patches of sea and shadow, and those only as blobs. You cannot tell there is a path, a cliff or a horizon. Hue and chroma decorate; value draws.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Value structure — Image Wiki
answer:
The painting as painted, full of gradients and detail
Our own reduction of it to three flat values


Vilhelm Hammershøi, Ida Reading a Letter, 1899. Public domain. The right panel is our own reduction of the left one to three flat greys — no gradients, no modelling, no detail.
Cover the left panel. The right one still says "a woman in black at a white door, a laid table in front of her, a dark floor": three masses, and the composition survives intact. Nothing that was thrown away — the modelling on her sleeve, the grain of the boards, the coffee pot's highlights — was carrying the picture.
The reduction also exposes something the painting hides. Her white apron falls in the same value band as the door behind her, so from the waist down she has no edge at all; only the black bodice separates her from the room. That is a thin margin, and it is the first thing to vanish if someone decides to brighten the shadows.
