instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Value structure — Image Wiki
answer:
Low key: everything but the face sits in the dark half
High key: everything but one figure sits in the light half


Rembrandt van Rijn, Self-Portrait, 1659 (National Gallery of Art, Washington). Alfred Sisley, Snow at Louveciennes, 1874. Both public domain.
In the Rembrandt, cap, coat and background all live in the bottom third of the scale, separated by steps so small you have to hunt for the edge between the shoulder and the wall; the face is the only thing allowed up the scale. In the Sisley the opposite: snow, sky and walls fill the top half, and the dark notes are few and small — the woman with the umbrella, the bare trunks, the fence at the bottom left. Your eye goes to the woman rather than to the fence, because she is the dark shape with white on every side of her.
Note what neither picture is. Neither is low in contrast: the Rembrandt runs from near-black to a bright forehead, the Sisley from white snow to those near-black accents. Key describes where the bulk of the picture sits, not how far apart its extremes are.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Value structure — Image Wiki
answer:
James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Silver—Battersea Reach, c. 1870–75. Public domain.
A whole picture made of three masses and almost nothing else: pale sky, mid-value river, near-black barge and foreground. There is no drawing to speak of — the crane and the far chimneys are flat silhouettes, the water has no detail at all — and it still reads as a river at night.
Run the last item on the checklist below on it. The darkest dark is the barge, the nearest thing and the one the composition is arranged around; the lightest light is the far sky. Both are where the picture is about. The few orange specks are worth noticing as the exception: strongly coloured, but barely different in value from the water around them, which is why they read as sparks and not as the subject.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Visual hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
Dark subject in a light field: Hiroshige, Kanbara, evening snow
Light subject in a dark field: Joseph Wright of Derby, The Alchemist


Utagawa Hiroshige, Kanbara, Evening Snow, from The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō, c. 1833–35 (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston). Joseph Wright of Derby, The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, 1771 (Derby Museum and Art Gallery). Both public domain.
Opposite polarity, identical result. In the Hiroshige the whole field is white snow and the darkest things in it are three small travellers — and that is where you land, on figures a few percent of the frame. In the Wright the field is a near-black vault and the brightest thing is the glowing flask at the lower right — and that is where you land, before you have noticed there are four people in the room.
Now check what does not pull in the Hiroshige: the grey sky across the top is darker than the snow and much bigger than the travellers, and it attracts nothing. A wide area of one even tone has no internal difference to offer. The pull comes from a local mismatch, not from a tone being dark, or bright, or large.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Visual hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
Gordon Parks, American Gothic, Washington, D.C. (Ella Watson), August 1942. Farm Security Administration / Office of War Information, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Size and brightness both lose here, which is why this frame is a good test of the list above. The broom is the largest object in the picture and one of the palest; the flag is larger still. Your eye went to her face — a few per cent of the area, darker than everything around it, and sitting near the middle of the frame.
Two things prop it up. Her face is the sharpest region in the frame: the flag's stars are visibly soft, so the lens is pointing at her and nothing else. And her glasses draw two small high-contrast rings around the eyes, which is where recognition emphasis is strongest of all.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Visual hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
One focal point: a single man on a store porch
Several competing: six men and a wall of signs on another store porch


Russell Lee, Man on porch of general store near Jeanerette, Louisiana, October 1938 (cropped by us to match the other panel's shape). Dorothea Lange, Country store on dirt road, Gordonton, North Carolina, July 1939. Both Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress; public domain.
The same subject twice — people on the porch of a rural general store, loud advertising behind them — with opposite hierarchies.
On the left there is one place to look and you found it immediately. Note how little the signs manage: "666 COLDS FEVER" is black lettering on white, the highest local contrast on that wall, and it still loses to a face in a shadowed hat. His only real competitor is the white sleeve of the man cropped at the left edge, which is why that edge keeps nagging.
On the right, say your landings out loud: the standing man in the white shirt, the Texaco star, the "Chesterfields Satisfy" panel, the Coca-Cola sign, then the row of seated men, none of whom outranks his neighbours. Every element is fine on its own. What is missing is a ranking, and without one the eye keeps circling. That is the mechanism behind "it looks busy" — not too much stuff, but no order to visit it in.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Visual hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
Dorothea Lange, Toward Los Angeles, California, March 1937. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Answer honestly: what did you look at first? Almost certainly the billboard, not the two men. The board is the whitest rectangle in a grey photograph, it has a hard black edge all round it, and it carries text — three of the strongest pulls stacked in one place. The men are dark clothes against a mid-grey road, a much smaller local difference, and they are facing away.
Lange wanted that competition; the caption is the joke. But the mechanism is the one that ruins ordinary photographs, and the dominant element here is not the subject. Cover the right third with your hand and the men become the picture immediately.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Visual hierarchy — Image Wiki
answer:
Marion Post Wolcott, Center of town, Woodstock, Vermont, "snowy night", 1940. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Two attractors ranked properly. The lamp wins outright: it is the only small patch of blazing white in a dark field, while everything else bright here is either large and even (the snowbanks) or small and dim (the shop windows at the right).
Then watch the second mechanism arrive. The trodden footpath, both snowbanks and the line of parked cars all run toward the lamp post, so convergence points where contrast already pulled, and the two agree. Cover the lamp with a fingertip: the frame goes aimless at once, though nothing else has changed.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Wayfinding is not signage — Image Wiki
answer:
Photo: Tom Page, Legible London sign, Villiers Street, 2025, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
One object, three layers, top to bottom. The yellow cap and walking figure are a brand beacon — you learn once that yellow-plus-walker means pedestrian information here, and you can then spot it at 50 metres without reading anything. Under it, the area name answers "where am I": STRAND, with Embankment station below. Then the directional panel, which is the decision-point information: River Thames and South Bank ahead, Westminster and the Houses of Parliament right, Victoria Embankment Gardens left.
The bottom two-thirds is the map panel, here reduced to "New map coming soon" — a fair reminder that a wayfinding system is a maintenance commitment, not a construction project.

instruction: Explain the visual construction and teaching point illustrated here. Topic: Wayfinding is not signage — Image Wiki
answer:
Photo: Robskedgell, Wayfinding monolith map in Stoke-on-Trent, 2023, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Cropped.
The Legible London pattern, exported to a different city — the same yellow cap and walker, the same area-name-then-destinations order. The panel headed "Walking from here" is the point: every destination is priced in minutes, not metres, and the list is ordered so you can scan for something that fits the time you have. Below it sit the two map scales, the wider planner above the local finder.

answer:
Pure geometry
Script and a sabre


Rand's own pair of examples (ID-001). Both public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
Left: three vertical bands. No picture, no letters, nothing to interpret. Right: a line of Arabic script above a sabre, dense enough that you cannot resolve it at 50 metres. Two opposite ideas of what a mark should be, and both identify perfectly, because in each case a population learned it.
Rand's point about flags is that this settles the argument about beauty: "The ugliest flag is beautiful if it happens to be on your side." What you feel when you look at a mark is mostly what you already feel about the thing behind it.

NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.2 (ID-006). Work of the US federal government, public domain.
Two signatures, not two logos. Top: the logotype with the agency name under it in Helvetica Light. Bottom: the same, plus a centre name in the heavier Helvetica Medium — the manual says the bolder weight is what makes the centre name read first even though the agency always comes above it. The mark is identical in both. Everything that changed is the words locked to it.

answer:
NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.9 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
The seal: a ring of type around a stippled planet, a hairline orbit and a scatter of stars. Count the separate elements, then compare with the four solid letters of the logotype on the same desk. The manual reserves the seal for award presentations and ceremonial events, and states that it should never be used alongside the logotype, because the two "are intended for different purposes and are visually incompatible when seen side by side."
That is the emblem trade-off, written by people who had to enforce it. Detail buys gravity and costs you every small application.
